10.1016/j.enconman.2026.121816.abstract: Renewable-powered green ammonia production is constrained by substantial waste-heat losses, strong nonlinear subsystem interactions, and scale-dependent economic penalties that limit its efficiency and viability. This study quantifies how integrating vapour absorption refrigeration cycle – based waste-heat recovery reshapes the thermodynamic, economic, and environmental optima of green ammonia production systems across plant capacities ranging from 10 to 50 MW. Process modelling and data-driven optimisation show that ammonia production is governed primarily by electrical input, whereas refrigeration capacity, revenue generation, and greenhouse-gas mitigation depend on the interplay between recoverable waste heat and refrigeration-cycle performance. When operated under capacity-specific optimal conditions, waste-heat recovery enables more than a 200 % increase in total system-level avoided greenhouse-gas emissions between 10 and 50 MW, relative to a system without waste-heat recovery. Energy and exergy efficiencies remain nearly constant, varying by less than 3 %. The analysis further identifies a pronounced scale effect in the levelised cost of ammonia. Increasing plant capacity reduces the LCOA by approximately 40 % up to 25 MW, beyond which the addition of parallel production units introduces a temporary cost penalty. Continued scaling offsets this penalty, yielding a further approximately 45 % reduction at 50 MW. These results demonstrate that optimal system performance cannot be inferred from monotonic scaling assumptions; rather, it depends on discrete capacity transitions and waste-heat utilisation strategies. A machine-learning surrogate coupled with multi-objective optimisation enables rapid identification of these optimal operating regimes while preserving thermodynamic consistency. Overall, the results establish waste-heat recovery as a scale-sensitive design lever for achieving economically viable and low-carbon green ammonia production.

The calculated stability descriptors reveal a strongly non-monotonic landscape, with several compositions locally favoured relative to neighbouring stoichiometries within the explored isolated-cluster model. Molecular NH$_3$ adsorption was examined at W-top and accessible B-top sites, with adsorption energies ranging from $-1.78$ to $-0.54$ eV on W sites and from $-1.54$ to $+0.62$ eV on B sites. H adsorption at W-top and B-top sites spans $-1.47$ to $+0.67$ eV, indicating pronounced composition- and site-dependence. CI-NEB calculations show that the first N-H bond-cleavage barrier is strongly pathway-dependent. These results characterize the initial activation of NH$_3$ on W-B nanoclusters and provide an atomistic basis for further investigation of the complete ammonia-decomposition mechanism.

10.1016/j.jcis.2026.141733.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (NO3RR) offers a sustainable route for ammonia synthesis but is hampered by the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and sluggish intermediate conversion at the catalyst-electrolyte interface. Herein, we report an amorphous Bi-doped cobalt sulfide (a-Bi-CoS) catalyst that addresses these challenges via tandem structure-electronic regulation of Co sites. The amorphous framework promotes uniform Bi incorporation and abundant BiS bonds, reconfiguring the local coordination environment and surface charge distribution of Co. In situ Raman/FTIR spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal that this tandem effect strengthens *NO adsorption, lowers the barrier of the rate-determining *NO → *NOH hydrogenation step, enhances water dissociation, and weakens *H binding. This tandem regulation kinetically favors protonation of nitrogen-containing intermediates and improves NO3RR selectivity. Consequently, a-Bi-CoS achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 94.3% and an NH3 yield of 18.02 mg h-1 cm-2 at -0.5 V vs. RHE. Integrated into a membrane electrode assembly flow reactor coupled with glycerol oxidation, it delivers a stable NH3 production rate of 23.58 mg h-1 cm-2 over 40 h, highlighting its great potential for practical electrochemical ammonia synthesis.

10.1016/j.jece.2026.123440.abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction (eNO3-R) has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional biological denitrification for nitrate wastewater treatment, enabling the recovery of ammonia as a value-added product while eliminating greenhouse gas emissions. However, systematic evaluations of downstream ammonia separation technologies integrated with eNO3-R remain insufficient. This study proposes and comparatively assesses five process configurations for ammonia recovery: conventional biological treatment as a baseline, atmospheric distillation, pressurized distillation, air stripping with acid trapping, and steam stripping with neutralization. Process simulations based on the Electrolyte Non-Random Two-Liquid (ENRTL) thermodynamic model were conducted, followed by comprehensive exergy analysis, techno-economic assessment, and sensitivity analysis. The exergy analysis revealed that air stripping achieved the lowest specific exergy destruction of 2.68 GJ/kmol-N, representing a 50% reduction compared to atmospheric distillation (5.34 GJ/kmol-N). The techno-economic analysis demonstrated that steam stripping attained the lowest unit treatment cost of 61.63 USD/kmol-N at the base-case capacity, followed by air stripping (67.51 USD/kmol-N), both outperforming the biological baseline (89.94 USD/kmol-N). Electricity consumption associated with the electrolyzer constituted the dominant cost component, accounting for 37–73% of direct production costs across all eNO3-R configurations. Scale-up analysis indicated that air stripping exhibits the most pronounced economies of scale, becoming increasingly cost-competitive at larger treatment capacities. These findings demonstrate that eNO3-R integrated with stripping-based ammonia recovery offers a viable pathway for transforming nitrate wastewater treatment from a cost-intensive disposal operation into a value-generating resource recovery process.

10.1016/j.jece.2026.124413.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction to ammonia (eNO3‐RR) is an eco-friendly technology for the treatment of nitrate (NO3‐)-polluted water. An optimized bimetallic metal-organic framework material of Cu0.33Co0.67-BDC (H2BDC = 1,4-benzene dicarboxylic acid) was proposed as an efficient electrocatalyst for eNO3‐RR with the outstanding NH3 yield of 207.68 μmol∙h‐1cm‐2 and faradic efficiency of 77.95 %. The electrocatalytic stability and durability of Cu0.33Co0.67-BDC for eNO3‐RR are demonstrated by NH3 yield and FE both fluctuating in an extremely narrow range during ten eNO3⁻RR cycles and a stable 10-hour amperometric current-time test. The electrocatalytic mechanism is revealed as a synergistic effect between Cu(II) and Co(II) active sites. Cu0.33Co0.67-BDC is also designed as an anode to construct with Zn metal as a cathode into a zinc-nitrate (Zn-NO3⁻) battery. The Zn-NO3⁻ battery outstands itself for electrical energy supply with an impressive open circuit voltage of 1.62 V (vs. Zn/Zn2+), a power density of 1.59 mW cm-2 and a limiting current density of 4.68 mA cm-2. Two series-connected Zn-NO3⁻ batteries can power four LEDs in parallel simultaneously, supporting the practical capability of electrical power supply. This work provides an innovative approach for developing integrated "NO3⁻-pollution removal-energy supply" technologies

10.1016/j.jece.2026.124468.abstract: Microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP) shows promising potential for coal dust suppression, but the byproduct ammonium pollution severely restricts its practical application. Herein, Sulfitobacter sp. IGS-18 was used to further simultaneously enhance coal dust suppression efficiency and in-situ byproduct ammonia removal capacity by enhancing the activity of urease, glutamine synthetase (GS), and glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). Enzymatic assays demonstrated that Mg²⁺ significantly enhanced the activities of the three enzymes, with maximum relative activities of 158.7% (urease), 289.9% (GS), and 194.83% (GDH). The optimal Mg/Ca molar ratio was 6.0, under which compact mineralized products consisting of Mg-doped calcite and magnesium carbonate were formed. The treated coal reached a maximum hardness of 52.8 HA, with wind erosion loss of 1.7% and rain erosion loss of 8.37%. Furthermore, Sulfitobacter sp. IGS-18 supplemented with Mg²⁺ attained 90.1% NH₄⁺-N removal efficiency and reduced NH₃ emission by 94.9% relative to conventional MICP employing Sporosarcina pasteurii. Molecular docking revealed that Mg²⁺ anchored to enzyme active sites via coordination bonds with conserved Asp and Glu residues, stabilizing enzyme conformations and promoting substrate binding. This study provides a novel bacterial resource and theoretical basis for developing eco-friendly biomineralization dust suppression technology in coal mining areas.

10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.131250.abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO3RR) to ammonia could couple nitrate removal with lower-carbon nitrogen recovery, but its eight-electron pathway makes activity and selectivity hard to control. A material-by-material view can hide how active-site structure, mass transfer and operating conditions work together. Here we assess NO3RR through a joint structure-activity and reaction-system framework. We compare facet-controlled Pd, evolving Cu/CuOx interfaces, Cu-Co tandem sites, isolated and symmetry-broken Fe centers, defect-rich Zr supports, metal-organic frameworks and other transition-metal systems. Across these materials, the evidence links selective ammonia formation to a matched sequence of nitrate capture, N-O bond cleavage, proton delivery, intermediate hydrogenation and product release. We also examine pulsed potentials, porous electrodes, flow cells and product recovery as ways to regulate transport and intermediate coverage beyond static catalyst design. However, reported metrics do not support a universal catalyst ranking because studies use different nitrate concentrations, electrolytes, potentials, cell designs and rate units. We therefore identify four priorities: direct tracking of active states during operation, shared testing rules, long-term tests with realistic feeds, and catalyst-reactor co-design at practical current densities. This framework connects atomic-scale catalyst design with device operation and sets clear tests for advancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion.

10.1016/j.wasman.2026.115813.abstract: The efficient and low-cost recovery of metal in fly ash (FA) is crucial for its resource utilization. However, because metals were present in the structurally stable mullite, the recovery processes impose significant environmental and cost pressures. This study proposes a Li-mediated Flash Joule heating (Li-FJH) method to transform mullite into an amorphous glass phase and LiAlSiO4, thereby enhancing the leaching behavior of FA. First, the effects of Li2CO3 dosage, FJH temperature and time on the mullite Li-FJH were investigated. The FJH product was leached using eco-friendly citric acid. The optimal concentration was identified and the leaching kinetics were fitted. Second, the phase composition, microstructure, chemical bonding structure, and changes in the coordination states of Al and Si in the FJH products were analyzed using XRD, SEM, RS, FTIR, and NMR to elucidate the mechanism of mullite transformation. The content of metal in leachate was determined by ICP-MS to evaluate the recovery efficiency of valuable components and Li inducer. Finally, the advantages of this approach were assessed. The results indicate heating at 1800 °C for 8 s effectively induced the transformation of mullite into an amorphous glass phase and LiAlSiO4. 99.12 % of Al, 99.64 % of Fe and 99.86 % of Li were leached using 0.75 M citric acid at 80 °C for 90 min. The leaching behavior of the FJH product conforms to the Avrami model. This method demonstrates advantages in energy consumption, processing and cost, offering a new strategy for the FA recovery.

10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c01663.abstract: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a van der Waals material with excellent insulating properties that make it well-suited as a gate dielectric in 2D electronic devices. In recent years, the discovery of an ever-increasing list of properties has led to a much broader range of potential applications, including quantum photonics, memristive devices, and extreme-environment coatings. However, current growth methods for hBN films are characterized by a narrow selection of substrates and high temperatures that require transfer and limit scale-up. Here, we report a remote plasma-activated approach to directly synthesize large-area hBN films on a diverse range of representative metallic, semiconducting, and amorphous insulating substrates. Specifically, we employ the spatial afterglow of an Ar/H2 plasma to activate ammonia borane, which enables the growth of thick (>30 nm), uniform, and stoichiometric films on substrates such as Si, SiO2, glass, fused silica, Mo, and Al. Systematic spectroscopic characterization reveals that hBN films can be grown as low as 300 °C. Furthermore, plasma afterglow-grown hBN films exhibit mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties on par with or exceeding those reported by alternate synthesis methods. These results establish plasma afterglow growth for the direct integration of hBN into a wide range of emerging technologies.

10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c02250.abstract: Abstract The AtomicLimits ALD/ALE database is a community resource that catalogues atomic layer deposition (ALD) and atomic layer etching (ALE) processes reported in the literature. While widely used, it currently captures only a small fraction of the available information, with limited process information per entry, and relies on manual curation. As ALD/ALE process development grows in demand and complexity, with many interdependent parameters and increasingly sophisticated chemistries such as for multicomponent films, decades of experimental and simulation knowledge remain locked across publications, supplementary files, and lab notebooks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs), offer a path to unlock this knowledge for data-driven analysis and process design, but realizing this potential depends on structured, machine-readable data. In this perspective, we propose a framework to evolve AtomicLimits into an AI-ready knowledge infrastructure that integrates literature-extracted, experimental, and simulation data through a community-defined schema, a structured template that specifies which data fields to capture and how to organize them. We outline the AI capabilities this enables, from structured querying to autonomous experimentation, and discuss the coordinated community effort required to realize this vision for the atomic-scale processing field.

10.1021/acs.energyfuels.6c03763.abstract: Abstract Practical direct air capture (DAC) demands a sorbent contactor that simultaneously delivers high active-material loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid regeneration─requirements that conventional sorbent architectures rarely satisfy together. Here, we present a woven fiber contactor that addresses these requirements by interlacing dry-fabricated zeolite Y/PTFE fibers with copper wire supports into a structured contactor. Compared to a stacked laminate configuration, the woven sorbent exhibited markedly more efficient mass transfer, yielding a narrower mass transfer zone (LMTZ = 4.4 mm and 11.1 mm at 50 sccm) and a steeper breakthrough front. This structural advantage translated into robust sorption performance, with CO2 capture capacity varying by only 11.7% across a 10-fold increase in feed flow rate (50–500 sccm, corresponding to superficial velocities 5.79 × 10–3 to 5.79 × 10–2 m/s) compared to 19.2% for the stacked laminate. The woven architecture further reduced pressure drop by 7- to 18-fold over a wide range of superficial velocities (1.16 × 10–2–5.79 × 10–1 m/s). The integrated copper wires enabled electrified temperature swing adsorption (e-TSA) with near-instantaneous heating, driving CO2 desorption within 1 min. Over 10 consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles, the module retained an average capacity of 1.01 mmol/gsorbent with less than 6.93% variance. Together, these results establish the woven fiber contactor as a scalable platform that unites high sorbent loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid electrified regeneration for energy-efficient DAC.

10.1021/acs.energyfuels.6c04416.abstract: Abstract Rare-earth engineering of CeO2 offers a route to enhance Ru-based catalysts for ammonia synthesis by tailoring oxygen vacancies and metal–support interactions. Herein, we systematically synthesized and benchmarked Ru catalysts supported on RE (=Gd, La, and Sm)-modified CeO2 under identical conditions to establish promoter-structure–activity relationships. Rare-earth incorporation increased the Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio, oxygen-vacancy concentration, and weak acidic sites, facilitating electron transfer to Ru, promoting N2 activation, and potentially facilitating interfacial hydrogen spillover. H2-TPD suggested improved hydrogen mobility and utilization at the Ru/CeO2 interface. Ru/GdCeO exhibited the highest NH3 synthesis rate of (19.80 ± 0.98) mmol g–1h–1 at 400 °C and 1.5 MPa, with an N2:H2 ratio of 1:2 and WHSV = 13,500 mL g–1 h–1, yielding 3.53 vol % NH3 in the reactor effluent. Such superior performance may be associated with optimized Ru-support interactions and abundant oxygen vacancies. These findings establish Gd as the most effective promoter for Ru/CeO2 under mild synthesis conditions.

10.1021/acs.iecr.6c03540.abstract: Abstract Ammonia (NH3) emissions pose significant risks to both the environment and human health, yet the efficient removal of low-concentration NH3 under mild conditions remains a considerable challenge. Herein, we report a Na-doped WO3 photocatalyst synthesized via a hydrothermal route, where Na incorporation stabilizes the metastable hexagonal WO3 phase through a channel-doping mechanism, consistent with previous studies on alkali-metal-modified hexagonal WO3. The stabilized hexagonal Na/WO3 exhibits a high specific surface area (65.68 m2·g–1) and enhanced NH3 adsorption affinity (DFT adsorption energy of −1.37 eV). Under full-spectrum irradiation, the optimized Na/WO3-1 catalyst achieves an NH3 removal efficiency of 80.4% within 120 min, significantly outperforming its monoclinic counterparts. This superior performance is attributed to the synergistic coupling of efficient charge separation and photothermal conversion, which elevates the catalyst surface temperature to 71.3 °C and facilitates NH3 oxidation kinetics. In situ DRIFTS analyses reveal that NH3 oxidation proceeds via a photoinduced internal selective catalytic reduction (photo-iSCR) pathway, which differs fundamentally from the conventional thermally driven iSCR mechanism. This work establishes a structure–activity relationship between channel-doping-induced phase stabilization and photothermal catalytic performance, providing a rational strategy for designing efficient WO3-based catalysts for low-temperature NH3 purification.

10.1021/acs.jpcc.6c05052.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical reduction of nitrate ions (NO3–) to ammonia (NH3) offers a sustainable and environmentally route for the recycling of nitrogen. However, the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) is limited by complex eight-electron transfer kinetics and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), resulting in low Faradaic efficiency and poor NH3 selectivity. Herein, we successfully synthesized a non-noble-metal Cu/CoAl-LDH-xh catalyst via an ion-exchange engineering strategy, in which monodispersed copper single atoms were anchored onto the aluminum metal defect sites of tannic acid-etched cobalt–aluminum layered double hydroxide (LDH). In situ spectroscopic characterization and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the presence of Co sites combined with the introduction of copper single atoms establishes an electron transfer channel, thereby promoting surface electron redistribution. The synergistic interaction between Co and Cu active sites optimizes the H* kinetics and mitigates the imbalance between H* supply and consumption typically encountered in single-site configurations. Such cooperation effectively suppresses the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and lowers the energy barrier for the dehydration-hydrogenation of *HNOH, thereby driving the efficient conversion of nitrate to ammonia. Under low-concentration nitrate conditions, this catalyst exhibits outstanding nitrate reduction performance, achieving a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 98% and an ammonia selectivity over 80%, which surpasses most reported non-noble-metal catalysts as well as some noble-metal-based counterparts. These findings offer profound insights into the design and application of single-atom-anchored metal hydroxides, particularly in advancing the electrocatalytic conversion of nitrate to ammonia.

10.1021/acs.jpcc.6c05418.abstract: Abstract Atomic layer deposition (ALD) of metal phosphates is increasingly explored for energy applications, yet the mechanisms governing phosphorus incorporation remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce two novel ALD processes for amorphous tantalum phosphate and titanium phosphate thin films using tris(dimethylamino)phosphine (TDMAP) as the phosphorus precursor and metal alkylamides as precursors. Both processes employ a four-step ALD cycle, consisting of TDMAP/O2-plasma and metal alkylamide/O2-plasma subcycles, and exhibit a pronounced temperature dependence, with the growth per cycle decreasing as the temperature increases from 150 to 300 °C. In situ characterization indicates ligand exchange reactions during the TDMAP pulse and enhanced P uptake at lower temperatures due to higher reactive site density. The resulting films deposited at 150 °C are a tantalum oxyphosphate and a phosphate-containing titanium oxide, both exhibiting substantially higher phosphorus-to-oxygen and phosphorus-to-metal ratios than their trimethylphosphate-based counterparts. A key finding of this work is that phosphorus incorporation can be further increased by replacing the O2-plasma pulse following the TDMAP exposure with a H2O pulse, shifting the composition toward phosphate-rich stoichiometries intermediate between ortho- and metaphosphates. In situ measurements suggest that less extensive ligand removal during hydrolysis reduces the availability of active sites for subsequent metal precursor adsorption, thereby lowering metal incorporation. These findings demonstrate that tuning the surface chemistry established between the TDMAP and metal precursor exposures provides a straightforward and effective approach for tailoring the composition of metal phosphate films.

10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c04121.abstract: Abstract Microwave-driven carbothermal shock (CTS) synthesis has attracted considerable attention as an ultrafast route for nanomaterial production. However, controlling nanoparticle nucleation and growth during the extremely short microwave irradiation period remains challenging. Although defect-rich carbon materials have frequently been employed in microwave-driven CTS synthesis, the influence of a separately introduced defect-containing surface layer on nanoparticle formation remains insufficiently understood. In this study, carbon cloth (CC) was coated with a polyacrylonitrile (PAN) solution and thermally oxidized at 200–400 °C to modify the surface carbon structure through the evolution of PAN-derived polyaromatic clusters prior to microwave irradiation. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated that increasing the oxidation temperature promoted the formation of larger and more ordered polyaromatic domains, accompanied by changes in the surface defect characteristics. These structural variations were associated with distinct Cu nanoparticle sizes and distributions following CTS synthesis. Among the investigated oxidation temperatures, the PAN-coated CC treated at 300 °C produced the smallest and most uniformly dispersed Cu nanoparticles, with an average diameter of 58 ± 25 nm. These findings suggest that controlling the structural evolution of PAN-derived surface carbon layers can provide a practical approach for regulating nanoparticle size and dispersion during microwave-driven CTS synthesis.

10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c04725.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia provides a sustainable route for nitrate-containing wastewater remediation and energy conversion. The development of nonprecious metal electrocatalysts that simultaneously achieve high ammonia selectivity, fast production rate and long-term stability still remains challenging. This study constructs hierarchical Cu–Co layered double hydroxide nanoarrays directly grown on nickel foam (CuCo LDH/NF) via a facile one-step hydrothermal method. The present work highlights two coupled core innovations: the Cu–Co bimetallic tandem catalytic mechanism and the mass transfer enhancement originating from the interlaced three-dimensional nanoarray architecture. Benefiting from electronic synergistic effect between Cu and Co, a tandem catalytic pathway is formed to suppress intermediate byproduct accumulation. Meanwhile, the in situ grown interlaced nanosheet arrays formed a hydrophilic, hierarchically porous three-dimensional open network. This architecture significantly enlarged the electrochemically active surface area (7.7 mF cm–2) and enhanced mass transfer efficiency. Owing to such dual synergistic optimization of catalytic active sites and mass transfer pathways, the as-prepared CuCo LDH/NF delivers a high NH3 Faradaic efficiency of 96.78% and an NH3 yield rate of 7.8 mg h–1 cm–2 at −0.9 V vs RHE in neutral electrolyte, alongside robust stability over 15 h continuous electrolysis. Kinetic analyses reveal that the nitrate reduction reaction follows an apparent pseudo-first-order model, and the reaction rate constant reaches 0.0521 min–1, which is approximately 23-fold higher than monometallic Co LDH catalyst. Furthermore, the catalyst exhibits good adaptability toward varied nitrate substrate concentrations within a certain range. This work offers a dual-regulation strategy combining electronic-structure modulation and mass-transfer intensification for designing high-performance nitrate-reduction electrocatalysts, and provides experimental insights for practical treatment of nitrate polluted wastewater.

10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c05296.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical nitrate reduction to ammonia requires a delicate balance between nitrate activation, hydrogen delivery, suppression of competing hydrogen evolution, and stabilization of the catalytic metal centers. Such coupled requirements make the rational design of dual-atom catalysts challenging, particularly when the two metal sites and their coordination environments contribute differently to the reaction. Here, we establish an interpretable active-learning framework to navigate the chemical space of asymmetric dual-atom catalysts and uncover the physicochemical origins of their performance. Rather than learning an empirical activity score, the framework predicts individual DFT-derived properties from readily accessible elemental and structural descriptors and uses uncertainty-aware sampling to iteratively explore previously uncharted metal-pair and coordination environments. Model interpretation reveals distinct roles of the two metal sites in regulating nitrate activation and hydrogen adsorption, and identifies moderate electronic asymmetry coupled with mixed N/O coordination as a favorable design regime. Guided by these principles, active learning efficiently explores an expanded library of 1050 structures and progressively identifies candidates beyond the initial chemical space. Prospective DFT validation highlights Mo–Ta/N3O3–C, Mo–Nb/N3O3–C, and Mo–Nb/N5O1–C as promising catalysts, whose performance arises from a balanced combination of reaction thermodynamics, adsorption selectivity, and structural stability. These findings establish a transferable strategy for designing multifunctional dual-atom sites and demonstrate how interpretable, closed-loop learning can transform catalyst screening from property prediction into mechanism-guided materials discovery.

10.1021/acsaem.6c01593.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (ENRR) is an environmentally friendly and sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) production. It offers a promising alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, significantly reducing its environmental impact. In this study, cobalt hydroxide nanoneedle arrays were successfully prepared on nickel foam (Co(OH)2@NF) by a facile hydrothermal approach. The Co(OH)2 structure was then overlayered simply by Au atoms through galvanic replacement. This process created a synergistic effect between Co and Au, which promotes N2 activation while suppressing the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that Au incorporation significantly modifies the electron density redistribution around adsorbed N2 molecules, creating more favorable sites for protonation and thereby enhancing the ENRR kinetics. The replacement of Co with Au atoms increased the Faradaic efficiency (FE) from 38.2 ± 2.4% to 90.1 ± 2.3%. The NH3 yield rate (rNH3) nearly doubled from 0.45 µg h−1 cm−2 ± 0.02 (2.00 × 10−8 mol h−1 cm−2) at –0.15 V vs RHE to 0.85 ± 0.06 µg h−1 cm−2 (4.98 × 10−8 mol h−1 cm−2) at a more favorable potential of + 0.00 V vs RHE. The Co(OH)2–Au@NF electrocatalyst can be used as a stable and effective electrocatalyst for the green synthesis of NH3, which is, to the best of our knowledge, among the highest FE values reported for ENRR under ambient conditions, particularly considering the extremely low overpotential.

10.1021/acsaem.6c02542.abstract: Abstract Modulation of the electric double layer (EDL) by different alkali metal cations (AMCs) is a powerful yet poorly understood strategy for steering the selectivity of the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) over the dominant hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) for ammonia synthesis. This study unveils a transformative mechanism for steering the selectivity of the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) over the dominant hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the charged Cu(111)/water interface using constant-potential ab initio molecular dynamics. This study examines the alkali metal cations (Li+, Na+, and K+) modulated proton dynamics near the electrified interface at –0.5 V vs RHE. The core discovery goes beyond the traditional spectator-ion paradigm by establishing a dynamic solvation descriptor. The results demonstrate that while Li+ remains trapped in the outer Helmholtz plane (OHP) due to a rigid hydration shell, K+ undergoes spontaneous partial desolvation, migrating into the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). This dynamic relocation provides direct electrostatic stabilization of the critical *NNH intermediate, lowering its activation barrier to 0.973 eV—a pathway inaccessible with Li+ or Na+. Furthermore, the presence of K+ in the IHP induces a catastrophic disruption of the interfacial hydrogen-bond network. By forcing an H-down water orientation, K+ physically deconstructs the proton-transfer pathways required for the competing HER. While Li+ and Na+ maintain multiple water orientations that promote hydrogen bonding, the steric gating effect of K+ effectively suppresses HER. These atomistic insights are consistent with experimental findings showing high NH3 Faradaic efficiency in KOH at –0.5 V vs RHE. By correlating cation desolvation kinetics with proton steric gating, this work identifies hydration-shell lability and local-field effects as the fundamental drivers of selectivity, offering a sophisticated roadmap for designing electrified liquid interfaces for sustainable ammonia synthesis.

10.1021/acsami.6c12867.abstract: Abstract Traditional metal heat sinks are limited by moderate thermal conductivity, high density, and poor flexibility, which restrict their use in compact and lightweight electronics. Graphene films offer high in-plane thermal conductivity, but rapid reduction of graphene oxide (GO) releases gases from oxygen-containing groups and can generate pores, interlayer damage, and poor film densification. Here, we report a precursor-design strategy that combines reduced graphene oxide nanosheets (GNs) with carboxylated cellulose nanofibers (CNFs). The composite films (GO/GNs-X) were prepared by blade coating, hot-press carbonization, and secondary Joule-heating graphitization. The combined precursor was designed to mitigate gas-release-induced damage and support carbon-network reconstruction during high-temperature treatment. The optimized GF, with a thickness of approximately 25 μm, reached an in-plane thermal conductivity of 950.5 ± 20 W m–1 K–1 and an electrical conductivity of 2.31 × 105 S m–1. At a comparable thickness, this thermal conductivity was 26.6% higher than that of an additive-free RGO-2600-ref film prepared without GNs/CNF modification. In LED heat-dissipation tests, the surface-centre temperature decreased from 83.7 to 40.4 °C. Because individual-additive controls were not included, the respective contributions of GNs and CNF could not be separated. These results establish combined precursor modification as a route to thin, lightweight graphene heat spreaders. Such films may be useful for thermal management in compact electronics, foldable devices, and aerospace systems.

10.1021/acsanm.6c04223.abstract: Abstract This study reports the continuous hydrothermal synthesis of Mg-doped Co3O4 spinel nanomaterials in supercritical water. By optimizing the synthesis parameters, crystalline MgxCo3−xO4 nanospinels (22−35 nm) were obtained directly at 391 °C with τ ≥ 0.1 s and a Mg/Co ratio of 0.25, without thermal post-treatment. Under these conditions, the formation of secondary (Mg,Co)(OH)2 phases was suppressed. Structural refinement indicates a moderately inverse spinel lattice, with Mg2+ incorporation limited to x ≤ 0.24, consistent with the formation of a thermodynamically stable Mg0.24Co2.76O4 spinel phase, as confirmed by HAADF-STEM-EDX analysis. Furthermore, the mixed oxides were evaluated as catalyst precursors for ammonia decomposition after reduction in H2 at 600 °C to generate active metallic cobalt particles embedded in a MgO matrix. Catalytic studies revealed that the performance is determined by a balance between reducibility and cobalt dispersion. On the one hand, increasing Mg content decreases the extent of reduction of the precursor, leading to a lower fraction of metallic cobalt in the catalyst. On the other hand, higher Mg concentrations improve the dispersion of metallic Co0 and its interaction within the MgO matrix, thereby suppressing metal particle sintering. This study demonstrates that precise control of the synthesis enables a detailed understanding of the phase formation in Co−Mg mixed oxides and establishes a reliable strategy for the continuous synthesis of catalyst precursors that yield highly efficient, sintering-resistant catalysts.

10.1021/acscatal.6c02659.abstract: Abstract Sluggish charge dynamics and poor *NO polarization at active sites hinder the efficiency of photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (PcNRA). To address these issues, an atomic-level regulation strategy synergizing facet engineering with axial coordination was developed. Specifically, isolated Cu sites were anchored onto an electron-rich, ultrathin BiVO4 substrate exposing (040) facets. Functionalized ligands featuring distinct donor heteroatoms (S, N, O) were then systematically introduced, yielding a series of single-atom catalysts (S/N/O-Cu/BVO) with tailored axial microenvironments. A comprehensive methodology combining multidimensional spectroscopy and computational chemistry was established to verify this single-atom axial coordination. Detailed analyses of characteristic binding energies and absorption edge shifts via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and synchrotron X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) identified localized coordination field effects. Crucially, these effects are distinct from conventional electronic metal-support interactions (EMSI), providing spectroscopic confirmation of successful axial ligand incorporation and guiding the prediction of their configurations. Building upon these spectral findings, density functional theory (DFT) models were constructed and optimized, conclusively validating the asymmetric axial coordination configurations within the system, specifically Cu-S2O1, Cu-N2O1, and Cu-O4. Catalytic evaluations demonstrated that S-Cu/BVO achieves the highest ammonia yield at 435 μmol·h–1·g–1. In-situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations elucidated the multidimensional synergistic mechanism driving this enhanced activity: (1) The prominently exposed (040) facets act as an interfacial electron sink, efficiently directing photogenerated electrons toward the Cu sites; (2) The axial S ligands reconstruct the electronic structure of the Cu centers via strong orbital coupling, thereby improving effective orbital overlap with nitrate; (3) The resulting asymmetric Cu-NO-S bridging configuration polarizes the critical *NO intermediate, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for the rate-determining step.

10.1021/acscatal.6c03505.abstract: Abstract Commercialization of electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) is hindered by limited catalyst performance, the lack of scalable electrochemical cell architectures, and an incomplete understanding of performance-limiting processes. This work aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of catalyst composition and microstructure, device configuration, and reaction mechanisms. Molybdenum (Mo) metal single atoms and clusters supported on mesoporous nitrogen-doped carbon were synthesized with tunable pore sizes via a five-second photothermal pyrolysis of a self-assembled bottlebrush block copolymer (BBCP) template. For eNRR, improved Mo dispersion enhanced electrochemical accessibility, while the coexistence of atomically dispersed Mo species and Mo clusters produced a structurally heterogeneous catalytic environment that benefits eNRR. A gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) flow cell was constructed for continuous operation testing; the catalyst–device system achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 21.6% and an ammonia yield rate of 34.7 μg h–1 mg–1. Intermediate pore sizes and balanced electrode wettability promoted effective triple-phase boundary formation and active-site utilization. Electrochemical characterization combined with machine-learning analysis of flow-cell parameters indicated that activation polarization is the dominant loss mechanism, governed primarily by intrinsic active-site kinetics and electrochemically accessible surface area. In contrast, pore size, metal dispersion, and electrode wettability primarily regulate site accessibility rather than mass-transport limitations. Together, these results provide a framework linking catalyst structure, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations in eNRR flow-cell systems and offer practical design guidelines for advancing scalable eNRR technology.

10.1021/acscatal.6c05587.abstract: Abstract Hetero-anion doping has emerged as an effective approach to modulate the physicochemical and catalytic properties of perovskite-type oxides. In this study, nanosized CeO2 synthesized by a continuous flow-type supercritical hydrothermal synthesis (SHS) process was employed as a precursor for a solid-state reaction with Ba(NH2)2, enabling the low-temperature synthesis of single-phase perovskite oxynitride–hydride BaCeO3–xNyHz (BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS) with a high surface area and abundant N3– and H– species. Ru-loaded BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS exhibited a maximum ammonia synthesis rate of 9.0 mmol g–1 h–1 at 300 °C and 0.9 MPa and showed up to a 6-fold enhancement in activity compared with the corresponding Ru/BaCeO3–xNyHz prepared from commercial CeO2, owing to the enhanced generation of anion vacancies at the Ru–support interface. Moreover, BaCeO3–xNyHz–SHS acted as a highly efficient support for various transition metals in ammonia synthesis and for Ni in ammonia decomposition, achieving >99% conversion at 560 °C with a low apparent activation energy (75 kJ mol–1). These findings demonstrate that enhancing the solid-state reactivity of oxide precursors through nanoscale engineering provides a general strategy for the low-temperature synthesis of highly active hetero-anion perovskite catalysts for ammonia synthesis and decomposition.

10.1021/acscatal.6c05790.abstract: Abstract Ammonia decomposition provides a promising route for on-demand hydrogen production, but conventional thermocatalytic systems are constrained by severe kinetic limitations at low temperatures, limiting their compatibility with low-grade heat utilization. Herein, we develop an electric-field-assisted oxygen-vacancy engineering strategy to promote low-temperature NH3 decomposition over Ru/CeO2 catalysts. Ru/CeO2 catalysts with tunable oxygen-vacancy concentrations were prepared via a pre-impregnation and solid-state grinding method. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations reveal that oxygen vacancies intrinsically strengthen Ru–CeO2–x interfacial electronic interactions, promote charge redistribution, and generate relatively electron-enriched Ru sites. More importantly, the applied electric field further amplifies this vacancy-mediated interfacial regulation and facilitates H-species transfer/removal. The optimized Ru/CeO2-OV3 EF catalyst achieves 35.3% NH3 conversion at 150 °C under a high GHSV of 30,000 mL gcat–1 h–1 and exhibits an electric-field-assisted apparent activation energy of only 12.28 kJ mol–1. In situ DRIFTS, TPD measurements, impedance analysis, and DFT calculations collectively suggest that defect-associated O sites near oxygen vacancies provide favorable accommodation sites for migrated H species, while the electric field promotes interfacial polarization and accelerates H transfer from Ru sites to the CeO2–x surface. This synergistic effect reduces H coverage on Ru active centers, regenerates available Ru sites for sustained NH3 activation, and enables stable low-temperature operation. This work clarifies how an external electric field amplifies oxygen-vacancy-mediated interfacial electron/H transfer and provides a rational strategy for efficient low-temperature hydrogen production from ammonia.

10.1021/acscatal.6c05926.abstract: Abstract The electrocatalytic co-reduction of nitrate (NO3−) and carbon dioxide (CO2) into urea represents a potential avenue for achieving efficient urea production. However, this process involves intricate C–N coupling reactions and faces a severe kinetic mismatch between the reduction pathways. This disparity typically leads to a disproportionate coverage of key C- and N-containing intermediates on the catalyst surface, resulting in dominant competitive side reactions. Herein, we report the design of a heterogeneous FeNi@AC catalyst that integrates isolated Fe single atoms and Fe–Ni dual-atom sites at the atomic scale, enabling the efficient conversion of NO3− and CO2 into urea. Combined experimental and theoretical investigations reveal that the isolated Fe single-atom sites retain high nitrate reduction capability. Crucially, the introduction of Ni induces an electronic reconfiguration of the Fe center, which significantly lowers the energy barrier for CO2 activation (from 0.7 eV to 0.1 eV). This activation effectively bridges the kinetic gap between C- and N-species. Consequently, the FeNi@AC catalyst achieves a urea yield rate of 13.6 mmol g–1 h–1 and a Faradaic efficiency of 51.7% at –0.8 V (vs RHE). This work not only presents an active catalyst for urea synthesis but also provides a site-specific regulation strategy for designing multifunctional atomic-site catalysts tailored for complex tandem reactions.

10.1021/acscatal.6c06060.abstract: Abstract Nitrate electroreduction links water purification with ammonia production, but its use is still limited by sluggish proton-coupled electron transfer, poor product selectivity, and competition from the hydrogen evolution reaction. Single-atom-based dual active sites (SADASCs) address these constraints by coupling atomically dispersed metal centres with adjacent single atoms, clusters, or nanoparticles. Such coupled motifs regulate adsorption, charge redistribution, intermediate stabilisation, hydrogen supply, and product release in a step-specific manner. This review discusses electrocatalytic nitrate reduction according to its elementary sequence: nitrate adsorption and activation, initial N–O bond cleavage, nitrite conversion, deep NOx hydrogenation, active-hydrogen regulation, product desorption, and catalyst reconstruction. SADASCs are then classified into single-atom/single-atom, single-atom/cluster, and single-atom/nanoparticle architectures, with emphasis on how dual-site coupling overcomes the limitations of isolated single atoms. Key challenges in stability, operando identification, selectivity control, benchmarking, matrix tolerance, and device integration are also summarized. This perspective provides design principles for dual-site catalysts that can promote nitrate valorization under complex aquatic conditions.

10.1021/acscatal.6c06098.abstract: Abstract The low-temperature high-efficient decomposition of ammonia, a carbon-free hydrogen carrier, is essential to the promising hydrogen energy storage. However, the decomposition is hindered by slow reaction kinetics due to dynamically hydrogen poisoning and thermodynamically high nitrogen recombination barrier in ordinary thermocatalysis. Herein, we propose a photothermocatalytic strategy to resolve these kinetic issues and achieve enhanced hydrogen production. Under full-spectrum light irradiance of 20 kW m–2, a hydrogen production rate of 4.2 mmol g–1 min–1 at 300 °C has been achieved over the Ru/CeO2–x catalyst, significantly outperforming conventional thermocatalysis. Insights from in situ characterizations and density functional theory calculations indicate that the enhanced performance is ascribed to photopromoted hydrogen spillover and nitrogen recombination, which are mediated by the strong metal–support interaction. On one hand, the photogenerated electrons promote the H dissociation over sub-nm Ru clusters and migration across the metal–support interface, and the photoinduced oxygen-vacancy-rich CeO2–x surface favors to spread the active H· species. On the other hand, the photogenerated electrons reduce the activation energy for Ru–N bond cleavage, which is beneficial for N–N recombination. This study has demonstrated the distinct advantage of photothermocatalytic hydrogen production as an energy-saving, high-efficient, and carbon-free route.

10.1021/acscatal.6c07016.abstract: Abstract Ammonia synthesis under mild conditions remains challenging because of the inertness of the N≡N bond and the limited ability of conventional catalysts to couple efficient dinitrogen activation with rapid hydrogenation. Here, we report a LiH/FePcG catalyst in which strong interfacial coupling between LiH and Fe–N–C sites enable efficient ammonia synthesis. Comprehensive characterization, including structural analysis, kinetic study, isotopic-labelling, gas-phase mass spectrometry, and in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) reveal that the catalytic activity originates from interfacial active sites. Under reaction conditions, structural nitrogen atoms within the Fe–Nx moieties undergo reversible consumption and reconstruction, demonstrating the dynamic participation of the Fe–N–C framework in ammonia synthesis. Concurrently, hydridic hydrogen supplied by LiH directly participates in the initial hydrogenation steps, while the LiH/Fe–N–C interface generates Fe-centered multicomponent hydride species essential for N2 binding and activation. An inverse H/D kinetic isotope effect, an H2-promoted 28N2/30N2 exchange rate, in situ spectroscopic evidence, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations collectively support a non-classical, hydrogen-assisted pathway for dinitrogen activation rather than the conventional direct N≡ bond cleavage. These findings establish interfacial hydride chemistry as a cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis and provide a strategy for designing advanced catalysts under mild conditions.

10.1021/acsenergylett.6c02477.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical ammonia synthesis via a lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) faces a fundamental selectivity challenge in which proton donors that accelerate productive protonation simultaneously promote parasitic hydrogen evolution. Here, we demonstrate that 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE), an amphiphilic alcohol, mitigates this limitation by decoupling thermodynamic acidity from kinetic reactivity. Despite its high acidity, TFE suppresses parasitic reactions through rapid interfacial passivation associated with its fluorinated structure, while modulating the microstructure of a fluoride-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Blending TFE with ethanol further optimizes proton activity and hydrogen bonding, yielding a thin, uniform SEI enriched in highly crystalline LiF with reduced interfacial resistance. The optimized electrolyte achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 59.0% in a continuous-flow reactor, maintained stable performance under potential-cycling, and reached 82.8% in a high-pressure batch reactor. This study highlights proton-donor engineering as a key strategy to modulate the SEI nanostructure for selectivity in Li-NRR.

10.1021/acsmaterialslett.6c00756.abstract: Abstract The recent discovery of molybdenum oxynitride (MoO2–x/Mo2N) being an effective plasmonic catalyst demonstrated potential for light-driven ammonia synthesis under ambient pressure. However, its preparation requires high-temperature ammonia annealing to introduce lattice nitrogen, increasing both cost and process complexity. Here, we investigate molybdenum oxide (MoO3–x), the precursor to synthesize MoO2–x/Mo2N, as a catalyst for ammonia synthesis. We show that molybdenum oxide undergoes continuous nitrogen incorporation during the reaction, accompanied by enhanced catalytic activity. Time-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals the emergence of nitrogen-containing surface environments. Thermal treatment is sufficient to induce this evolution, which approaches a relatively stable state after several hours. Notably, both molybdenum oxide and pre-synthesized MoO2–x/Mo2N develop similar nitrogen-containing surface chemical environments under reaction conditions. These findings demonstrate that the catalyst surface dynamically evolves during ammonia synthesis and that nitrogen incorporation is closely associated with enhanced catalytic activity.

10.1021/acsnano.6c11507.abstract: Abstract Real-world mixed textile waste streams seriously hinder recycling. Herein, we present a two-step flash Joule heating (FJH) strategy for directly upgrading mixed textile waste into ordered multilayer nano onion-like fullerenes (NOLFs). The interaction between different fibers, termed a “scaffolding effect” involving physical confinement and chemical bonding, was strengthened by the precarbonization (280 °C) treatment. Consequently, the polyester/cotton mixture can be upgraded to NOLFs within 5 s with high quality (I2D/IG = 1.47) and yield (41.6%) at 2000 °C, and this technology can be successfully extended to other textiles and solid wastes (polyamide, straws, etc.). The evolution pathway of carbon atoms leading to the formation of the core pentagonal/hexagonal ring structure in NOLFs was systematically investigated in this work. Moreover, an automated FJH prototype was developed to produce NOLFs with 86.4 g·day–1 continuously, and these NOLFs derived an excellent performance as electrode and lubricant.

10.1021/acsomega.6c07548.abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N2), as the most abundant gas in the atmosphere, poses a long-standing challenge in chemistry and biochemistry due to its high bond energy (≈941 kJ·mol–1) and thus low reactivity under mild conditions. In nature, nitrogenase can reduce N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, while industry relies on the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process for ammonia synthesis. This paper systematically reviews the mechanisms and catalytic progress in biological nitrogen fixation and industrial ammonia synthesis, with a focus on the structure and catalytic mechanism of nitrogenase, as well as the catalytic mechanisms and green pathways for industrial ammonia production. It further summarizes the design strategies and recent advances in artificial nitrogen fixation catalysts inspired by nitrogenase. For example, a biomimetic iron–molybdenum dual-atom catalyst on carbonized delignified wood (FeMo-CDW) recently achieved an NH3 production rate of 336.03 μg·h–1·cm–2 under acidic conditions, while an Fe single-atom catalyst supported on monolayer MoS2 delivered an NH3 production rate of 97.5 ± 6 μg·h–1·cm–2, underscoring the practical promise of nitrogenase-inspired systems. By reviewing molecular catalysts, metal sulfides/carbides, single-atom catalysts, and related directions, this review paper outlines future development pathways for efficient nitrogen fixation catalytic systems under mild conditions, offering theoretical insights and design principles for breakthroughs in green ammonia synthesis technologies.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c05454.abstract: Abstract Nitrate electroreduction to ammonia (NRA) has emerged as a promising green alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, offering a dual-benefit strategy for mitigating nitrate pollution while enabling carbon-neutral ammonia synthesis. However, its intrinsic multi-step proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) faces a fundamental issue, which requires achieving the selective coupling of nitrogen intermediates (*NHxOy) with protons (*H) while simultaneously suppressing parasitic side reactions. To address this, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to rationally screen the hybridization of Ru 4d and O 2p orbitals in oxygen-deficient RuO2, systematically evaluating it as a decisive descriptor for the adsorption characteristics of key intermediates. Building on this theoretical guidance, we synthesized monolayered RuO2 nanosheets through wet-chemical exfoliation, with oxygen-vacancy (Ovac) mediation to precisely modulate the targeted d–p hybridization. As a result, the RuO2 nanosheet with high Ovac (RuO2-HO) achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 94.3% and a production rate of 466.4 mmol h–1 g–1 at –0.4 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), outperforming its low-Ovac counterparts (RuO2-LO) by approximately fivefold. Complementary operando investigations and DFT calculations demonstrate that the optimized d–p hybridization in RuO2-HO balances the binding strengths toward *NHxOy and *H, thereby promoting nitrate activation and facilitating subsequent N–H coupling steps. This DFT-guided, vacancy-mediated d–p hybridization engineering establishes a versatile paradigm for the design of high-performance NRA electrocatalysts.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c05529.abstract: Abstract Developing a highly efficient photocatalytic nitrogen fixation system for sustainable ammonia synthesis represents a crucial strategy for advancing green energy conversion and modern agriculture. Inspired by the structural and functional features of natural nitrogenase, a heterojunction photocatalyst composed of MIL-53(Fe) and ball-milled graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) was rationally designed and constructed. The ball-milling process effectively introduced additional surface defects into g-C3N4, thereby enhancing N2 adsorption and facilitating charge carrier migration. Meanwhile, MIL-53(Fe) provided Fe-centered coordination sites that acted as biomimetic active centers. The intimate interfacial contact between MIL-53(Fe) and defect-engineered g-C3N4 established a bioinspired “metal-nonmetal” synergistic catalytic interface, closely resembling the cooperative mechanism of natural nitrogenase. Photocatalytic evaluations revealed that the optimal MIL-53(Fe)/g-C3N4 heterostructure (CNMIL-2) exhibited a markedly improved nitrogen reduction performance under visible-light irradiation, achieving an ammonia yield of 113.86 μmol·g–1·h–1, which was substantially higher than those of either component alone. The enhanced activity can be ascribed to the defect-mediated charge transfer, efficient spatial separation of photocarriers, and the synergistic interplay between Fe active centers and nitrogen adsorption sites. Moreover, the photo catalytically generated ammonia water fertilizer was directly applied to wheat seedling cultivation. The treated seedlings displayed significantly increased germination rates and accelerated early-stage growth, demonstrating the agricultural potential of the photo catalytically synthesized ammonia as a sustainable nitrogen source. This work provides new insights into solar-driven green ammonia synthesis, paving the way toward low-carbon and sustainable agricultural development.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c06287.abstract: Abstract Developing effective electrocatalysts that can convert low-concentration nitrate (NO3–) into ammonia (NH3) in dilute electrolytes remains a major challenge. In this work, high-performance atomically dispersed CuCo catalysts (CuCo-ADCs) were prepared using a hydrothermal route. When tested in electrolyte containing 50 ppm NO3–-N and 5 mM K2SO4 (supporting electrolyte), the catalyst delivered a high NH3 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 92.15%, ammonia selectivity of 96.33%, and NH3 production rate of 281.28 μg h–1 cm–2 at –0.6 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Electrochemical measurements indicated reduced solution diffusion resistance for this catalyst. After 10 h of continuous operation, more than 85% of the initial catalytic activity could be retained. Mechanistic characterizations suggested that the atomic-level dispersion accelerated reaction kinetics and suppressed the competing hydrogen evolution reaction. Such improvement originated from the optimized *NO3 adsorption and decreased N═O bond dissociation energy through bimetallic synergy. Within this catalytic system, Cu drove the nitrate reduction reaction, Co was responsible for key bond cleavage, and Ni promoted hydrogenation steps as well as product desorption. This study offers alternative design ideas for atomically dispersed catalysts intended for resource recovery from low-concentration nitrate-rich wastewater. The present catalytic system may be applied for simultaneous nitrogen removal and ammonia generation in practical wastewater treatment.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c08592.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical transformation of nitrate (NO3–) into ammonia (NH3) offers an environmentally sustainable pathway to complete the nitrogen cycle, enabling both green NH3 synthesis and NO3– pollution remediation. Herein, we propose an in situ synergistic reconstruction strategy for fabricating a Cu2O@Co-carbon nanofibers (CNFs) pre-electrocatalyst, integrated with the glycerol oxidation reaction (GOR) to replace the energy-intensive oxygen evolution reaction (OER), thereby significantly reducing energy consumption toward electrocatalytic NO3–-to-NH3 conversion. The potential-dependent reconstruction gives rise to coexisting Co0 and Co(OH)2 species together with active Cu sites. Electrochemical measurements and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support their complementary roles in *H generation and NO3– activation, respectively, thereby promoting the NO3RR while suppressing competing reactions. The resulting catalyst delivers an exceptional NH3 yield rate of 61.0 mg cm–2 h–1 at industrial-level current density, manifesting outstanding catalytic performance. This study offers a novel design principle and a reliable strategy for developing high-efficiency non-noble-metal-based bifunctional electrocatalysts and advanced coupled electrochemical systems.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c08616.abstract: Abstract As a promising strategy for green synthesis, tandem electroenzymatic catalysis has recently emerged. This work designs a tandem electroenzymatic catalysis platform by directionally immobilizing ionic liquid modified chloroperoxidase (CPO-ILEMB) onto silver-loaded reduced graphene oxide (Ag/rGO) modified with polyethyleneimine (PEI), thereby constructing the CPO-ILEMB/Ag/rGO-PEI bioconjugate for NO3– reduction reaction (NO3–RR). Firstly, Ag/rGO-PEI electrocatalytically reduces NO3– to NO2–. Subsequently, CPO-ILEMB converts NO2– to NH4+ with high substrate selectivity and catalytic specificity. PEI covalently immobilizes enzyme molecules via glutaraldehyde, enhancing their stability, and its protonated form provides positive charges to enrich NO3– and the intermediate NO2–. In situ FTIR analysis reveals that the NO2– intermediate is rapidly consumed at the CPO-ILEMB/Ag/rGO-PEI interface, accompanied by the accumulation of NH4+ species, verifying the successful construction of this tandem electroenzymatic system. As a result, the CPO-ILEMB/Ag/rGO-PEI bioconjugate achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 94.97% and an NH4+ yield rate of 4.94 mg h–1 mgcat–1 at –0.56 V vs. RHE, representing an NH4+ yield rate of 19.8-fold increase over Ag/rGO-PEI, and maintains stable performance during 216 h of continuous operation.

10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c10020.abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic nitrogen reduction provides a sustainable pathway for ammonia synthesis, but its efficiency in pure water is limited by rapid charge recombination, insufficient nitrogen activation, and slow proton coupled electron transfer (PCET). Herein, a copper ion-guided self-assembly strategy is used to construct vanadium-doped polyoxometalate-based two-dimensional nanosheets (PMo12-xVx-TTAB-Cu, x = 0–2). TTAB intercalation promotes the formation of a layered structure and enhances nitrogen adsorption, while copper ion bridging establishes Cu–O–Mo/V interface channels for directional charge transport. In situ Kelvin probe force microscopy and quasi in situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy show that photoexcited electrons preferentially migrate from Mo/V centers to Cu sites, facilitating charge separation and generating electron-rich Cu centers to activate N2. Vanadium doping further enhances electron buffering capacity and PCET kinetics, thereby promoting N2 hydrogenation. Therefore, PMo10V2-TTAB-Cu achieved an NH3 generation rate of 667.12 μmol g–1 h–1 in pure water, which is 1.7 times and 3.8 times higher than that of PMo11V-TTAB-Cu and PMo12-TTAB-Cu, respectively. In situ DRIFTS and DFT calculations revealed the lateral adsorption configuration of nitrogen and the alternating hydrogenation pathway, in which vanadium doping lowered the key hydrogenation energy barrier. This study demonstrates an efficient strategy for integrating interfacial charge regulation with electronic structure engineering toward efficient solar driven nitrogen fixation.

10.1021/jacs.6c06380.abstract: Abstract Ba3AlO4-xNyHz with an antiperovskite structure is employed as a support for transition-metal catalysts for ammonia synthesis. This metastable material is synthesized by employing multiple anions with different valences and ionic radii. The optimized non-noble metal catalyst, Co(5.8 wt %)/Ba3AlO4-xNyHz/Al2O3, exhibits an exceptional ammonia synthesis rate of 15.9 mmol g–1 h–1 at 0.9 MPa and 300 °C, outperforming benchmark Cs–Ru/MgO, industrial Fe catalyst, and recently reported non-noble metal catalysts. Structural analyses show that Ba3AlO4-xNyHz and Co species self-organize on γ-Al2O3 nanorods to form a hierarchically structured catalyst. Combined experimental and density functional theory analyses reveal that the high activity originates from incorporated (N2)− ions at Co–Ba–Al interfacial sites, where the combination of Ba and Al plays distinct roles in N2 activation and NHx formation, respectively. These findings not only provide a strategy for stabilizing metastable crystal structures through the incorporation of diverse anionic species but also demonstrate a unique cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis mediated by highly activated molecular (N2)− ions.

10.1021/jacs.6c16392.abstract: Abstract We present a systematic study of noble metal (Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh) single-atom cocatalysts decorated on p-type and quantum-confined TiO2 nanotubes for photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia. All single-atom cocatalysts were prepared through a reactive deposition using different metal precursors, resulting in a single-atom oxidation state (δ+) of δ ≈ 2. At a similar loading concentration (0.2–0.3 at%) and in the absence of any sacrificial agent, Pd single atoms exhibit the highest element-specific activity for ammonia production, while Pt single atoms display a prominent photocatalytic activity with a strong tendency of nitrite reduction toward ammonia. Rh single atoms achieve the highest ammonia selectivity, whereas Ir single atoms predominantly produce nitrite due to inhibited subsequent reduction. Comparisons with single atoms deposited on conventional TiO2 (P25) and with nanoparticles supported on the nanotubes reveal that both the semiconductor properties (quantum confinement effect and p-type conductivity) and the speciation of the cocatalyst (single atom) can significantly enhance activity and selectivity. These findings aid in establishing design principles for different single-atom catalysts toward efficient and selective photocatalytic nitrogen valorization.

10.1021/jacs.6c18484.abstract: Abstract Ammonia, an emerging energy carrier, demands advanced catalysts for synthesis under mild conditions to integrate with green hydrogen. We herein establish a family of metal fluoride supports (MFn, M = Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, or Ba) as a tunable “all-in-one” platform for ruthenium (Ru) catalysts. These Ru/MFn systems unify the critical merits of various existing catalysts, such as support-mediated activation of reactants and air stability. Varying the host cation can direct the catalytic pathway. Consequently, Ru/NaF exhibits excellent turnover frequency, while Ru/BaF2 delivers an NH3 synthesis rate of 58.0 mmolNH3 gcat–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 0.9 MPa─surpassing all reported Ru-based catalysts with ≤4 wt % Ru and without external promoters. Advanced characterization reveals that the fluorine vacancy formation energies of the alkali and alkaline-earth lattices, together with the vacancy-reactant interactions, dictate the divergent catalytic mechanisms mediated by different active sites. This work expands the chemistry of metal fluorides, launching a new paradigm for potentially viable NH3-synthesis under mild conditions.

10.1021/jacsau.6c01238.abstract: Abstract Driven by the growing need for sustainable ammonia production and effective nitrate remediation, the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has emerged as a promising technology. This process enables the conversion of nitrate pollutants into ammonia under mild operating conditions, offering a greener alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch route. However, the complex multielectron and multiproton transfer pathways involved in NO3RR require catalysts capable of precisely regulating intermediate adsorption, activation, and transformation. Atomically precise metal nanoclusters (NCs), with their well-defined atomic structures, tunable electronic properties, and identifiable active sites, have recently attracted considerable attention as model catalysts for elucidating structure–activity relationships. This perspective discusses the fundamental aspects of NO3RR, including key intermediates and reaction mechanisms, and summarizes recent advances in the use of atomically precise metal NCs for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. The catalytic performances of mono-, bi-, and trimetallic NCs are systematically compared, highlighting the roles of active-site engineering, ligand modulation, heterometal incorporation, and cluster assembly in regulating activity and selectivity. The perspective concludes by discussing the key challenges that remain in this field and highlighting future research directions toward the development of NC-based electrocatalysts with enhanced activity, selectivity, and long-term stability for sustainable ammonia production.

10.1021/jacsau.6c01315.abstract: Abstract Ammonia offers a carbon-free route for hydrogen storage and transport, but decentralized hydrogen supply requires efficient and rapidly responsive cracking technologies. Here, we integrate a warm plasma with Co/MgO–La catalyst to enable ammonia-to-hydrogen conversion without external catalyst heating. At a pure NH3 flow rate of 4 L min–1, the system achieves 99.5% conversion and reaches near-complete conversion within only 6 min after ignition, demonstrating rapid response characteristics, reproducible on–off cycling, and the potential for flexible operation under dynamic electrical inputs. Spatially resolved kinetic analysis and in situ intermediate detection reveal a plasma–thermal–catalytic relay, in which warm plasma generates NHx/H species and localized thermal energy through electron-impact activation and H-radical-mediated thermochemistry, while the downstream catalyst completes the conversion of unreacted NH3 and intermediates. Techno-economic and life-cycle assessments further indicate process-level advantages for this route. This work provides a rapidly switchable platform for distributed and on-demand hydrogen production from ammonia.

10.1038/s41598-026-73907-8.abstract: Abstract Ammonia is a vital commodity of key importance for global agriculture, but its traditional synthesis via the energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process features a high ecological footprint, contributing to ≈2% of the overall carbon dioxide emission. An eco-friendly and sustainable alternative is offered by electrochemical NO 3 − reduction (e-NO 3 RR), enabling also to simultaneously reduce the concentration of nitrate, a widespread water pollutant. Herein, we report on the ultra-dispersion of CuFe 2 O 4 , NiFe 2 O 4 , or Fe 2 O 3 nanoparticles (NPs) on graphitic carbon nitride (gCN), yielding heterostructured oxide@gCN systems as potential e-NO 3 RR catalysts. The target materials, fabricated by gCN electrophoretic deposition on carbon cloth (CC), followed by radio frequency (RF)-sputtering of oxide NPs in very low amounts, were subjected to a multi-technique characterization aimed at investigating their morphological, structural, compositional, and optoelectronic properties. The results indicate that gCN provides a robust, electronically coupled scaffold anchoring ultra-dispersed oxides, and evidence a gCN → oxide electron donation. Electrochemical tests coupled with ion chromatographic analyses highlight CuFe 2 O 4 @gCN as the best-performing catalyst, affording a Faradaic efficiency towards NH 4 + of 21% at -1.15 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), together with a comparatively higher ammonium production rate and reduced NO 2 − generation. Altogether, our results may pave the way to the potential implementation of functional catalysts for ammonia generation from nitrate‑containing aqueous media.

10.1039/d6cc04430a.abstract: Metal-free carbon materials are important electrocatalysts for two-electron oxygen reduction toward H 2 O 2 production owing to their low cost, good conductivity and tunable surface chemistry. Herein, we report flash Joule heating (FJH)-engineered multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) for selective H 2 O 2 electrosynthesis. FJH induces partial wall exfoliation and structural reconstruction of MWCNTs, enabling the simultaneous regulation of oxygen-containing defects, edge site exposure and graphitic conductivity. The sample treated at 1200 °C (denoted as MWCNTs-1200) preserves abundant oxygen-containing defects while exposing additional edge sites through partial wall exfoliation, providing a balanced structure for efficient 2e - ORR. MWCNTs-1200 delivers an H 2 O 2 production rate of 10.57 mol g cat -1 h -1 at 200 mA cm -2 with a Faradaic efficiency of 85%, and maintains stable operation for 10 h at 100 mA cm -2 , with the Faradaic efficiency decreasing only moderately from 94.6% to 82.2%. This work highlights FJH as an effective strategy to regulate CNT structure for efficient H 2 O 2 electrosynthesis.

10.1109/tste.2026.3693213.abstract: The wind-powered green hydrogen-to-ammonia system offers a promising pathway for utilizing marine renewable energy; however, its economic viability is constrained by the strongly nonlinear dynamics of ammonia synthesis and the inherent stochasticity of wind power generation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a bilevel scheduling framework. In the upper layer, a reduced-order Trend- and Structure-constrained Physics-Informed Neural Network (TS-PINN) model is developed by embedding trend priors and mechanistic constraints, effectively capturing the nonlinear characteristics of the ammonia synthesis process with significantly reduced computational effort. An improved Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization (MOPSO) algorithm is then employed to co-optimize operational strategies and key reactor setpoints, including bed temperature and pressure. In the lower layer, a Wasserstein-distance-based distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model is established to coordinate hydrogen production and storage operations to hedge against wind power uncertainty. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an effective balance among modeling accuracy, economic performance, and operational robustness, while accounting for coupled reaction–heat-transfer dynamics and renewable generation uncertainty.

10.1116/6.0005731.abstract: Hydrogenated silicon oxycarbide (SiOC-H) is a common low-permittivity dielectric material used in integrated circuits. As integrated circuits continue to downsize, SiOC-H deposition processes, such as molecular layer deposition (MLD) that offers precise thickness control and high conformity, are increasingly vital. MLD of SiOC-H using bis(trichlorosilyl)methane and water satisfies these demands via self-limiting surface reactions. Herein, we introduce the use of pyridine in the precursor dosing step to catalyze SiOC-H MLD, resulting in a growth per cycle of 0.31 nm/cycle, twofold increase over previously reported, and tenfold increase over observed under identical conditions without the presence of catalysts. Upon annealing at 250–550 °C, the Si–CH2–Si and Si–OH groups in SiOC-H undergo intramolecular reactions to form terminal Si–CH3 groups. These Si–CH3 groups decrease the density and dielectric permittivity (from ∼8 to 3.55). Water contact angle measurements reveal that annealing induces a transition in the SiOC-H surface from being hydrophilic to hydrophobic, which also enhances its etch resistance against diluted hydrofluoric acid solution. We compare the etch selectivity of as-deposited and annealed SiOC-H with that of silicon dioxide during CHF3/Ar reactive ion etching. Overall, our findings advance the practicality of SiOC-H MLD for the fabrication of nanoelectronics.

10.1116/6.0005783.abstract: Phosphorus-containing hybrid organic-inorganic materials demonstrate unique physicochemical properties making them suitable candidates for energy storage, electrocatalysis, and as protective and biocompatible coatings. Of special interest in this regard are metal phosphonate films, where the organic group bound to the P atom can tune functional properties of the films. However, the deposition of such materials in thin-film form remains challenging and has achieved only limited success. In this work, we present two deposition processes employing combination of atomic and molecular layer deposition approaches for the growth of aluminium phosphonates, utilizing trimethylaluminum as the Al source, and dimethyl methylphosphonate and dimethyl phenylphosphonate as the P sources, respectively. Both processes demonstrated saturated growth, and the incorporation of the phosphonate groups was confirmed using ex situ x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. As-grown films demonstrated a P/Al ratio of ca. 0.2–0.3, indicating the formation of a phosphonate-doped alumina matrix. Through density functional theory calculations, we delineated differences in precursor chemistry and their impact on growth characteristics for the processes. These films deposited using these approaches demonstrated superior thermal stability (≥500 °C) and hydrolytic stability under all tested conditions. The findings of this study can inspire the development of efficient processes for the incorporation of organophosphorus groups in such hybrid thin films.

10.1117/12.3114653.abstract: Thermal atomic layer etching (ALE) provides a precise pathway for aluminum surface preparation, optimizing optical performance at vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) wavelengths. This study investigates using trimethylaluminum (TMA) and anhydrous hydrogen fluoride (HF) to remove native aluminum oxide prior to encapsulation with dielectric thin films via atomic layer deposition (ALD). This integrated ALE/ALD process enables high-reflectance coatings and bandpass filters for applications below 200 nm. We demonstrate that the Al2O3 etch rate is highly sensitive to chamber conditioning; specifically, alkali halides like cesium fluoride catalyze the reaction. This effect lowers the thermal threshold for etching from >300 °C to 125 °C, protecting sensitive substrates and minimizing subsurface damage. While deep etching can increase roughness, lower temperatures enhance selectivity for native oxide removal. Consequently, a VUV mirror with ALD MgF2 improves from 60% to 80% reflectivity at 120 nm using this method. We discuss applications in electronics, superconductors, and the scalability of these methods for meter-class mirrors intended for future NASA large-aperture space observatories.

10.1117/12.3114668.abstract: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories advance microelectronics through coordinated programs and premier user facilities that connect fundamental science with technological innovation. This talk will overview key microelectronics research at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL), focusing on next-generation extreme ultraviolet (EUV) photoresists and atomic layer deposition (ALD) of interconnect and dielectric materials for highly scaled semiconductor devices. These efforts leverage BNL’s DOE user facilities, including the Center for Functional Nanomaterials (CFN)—one of five DOE Nanoscale Science Research Centers (NSRCs)—with expertise in ALD-enabled hybrid material synthesis for EUV lithography, and the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II) for advanced structural and chemical characterization. Recent progress in vapor-phase synthesis of organic-inorganic hybrid EUV resists and their patterning performance will be presented, along with studies clarifying ALD growth of ruthenium for advanced interconnects and dielectric deposition on two-dimensional (2D) materials for future channel applications.
