10.1117/12.3114726.abstract: Semiconducting 2D materials such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) show promising capabilities in use as field effect transistors, memory devices, and photodetectors, many of which structures require the addition of a dielectric top layer. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a well established method for producing dielectric films, however this process presents a problem for 2D materials as ALD relies on active surface chemistry that is generally not provided by 2D materials. Over enough ALD cycles, a dielectric film will eventually form on 2D materials by edge nucleation, however this loses ALD’s control over the film’s composition and thickness. In this study, we explore aluminum-flouride (AlFx) as a dielectric material deposited directly on MoS2. As the most electronegative element fluorine is expected to be more reactive than oxygen, potentially generating uniform nucleation sites on the 2D material’s surface. Preliminary results indicate that AlFx is capable of depositing directly onto exfoliated MoS2 within 5 ALD cycles. Research is ongoing to determine if ALD of AlFx causes any damages to the underlying MoS2. and to determine if 1 nm of AlFx is capable of fully covering MoS2.

10.1142/s3060932126300076.abstract: Electrochemical ammonia synthesis offers a promising sustainable alternative to the Haber–Bosch process, but progress remains fragmented across catalysis, ammonia validation, and reactor engineering. This review investigates an integrated framework combining catalyst design, reaction mechanisms, analytical validation, and reactor engineering to interlink the activation of nitrogen with consistent ammonia verification for high-yield ammonia synthesis. The roles of electronic structure, defect chemistry, active sites, interfacial effects, and electrolytes promote nitrogen activation and ammonia selectivity and inhibit the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction. Conventional electrochemical nitrogen reduction and alternative pathways, including nitrate and nitrite reduction, plasma-assisted synthesis, and lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction, are critically compared using common performance criteria encompassing reaction mechanisms, ammonia productivity, Faradaic efficiency, energy consumption, stability, and scalability. Specifically, the review pays attention to a critical assessment of ammonia quantification methods, which include colorimetric techniques, ion chromatography, nuclear magnetic resonance, and isotope labeling to reduce errors in ammonia quantification. The review further bridges catalyst-level performance and practical reactor operation by evaluating flow cells, gas-diffusion electrodes, membrane-based and zero-gap configurations, and stack architectures in terms of mass transport, current density, reactant utilization, product separation, and energy efficiency. Finally, this review identifies the energy barriers in the engineering to transition from laboratory scale to scalable ammonia generation.

10.15294/jese.v5i2.29164.abstract: Landfills are one of the causes of environmental pollution resulting from the disposal of human activity waste without further treatment (Yusri et al., 2020). In 2023, the total waste generation reached 1,270.00 tons per day, with 900 tons of waste being transported to the landfill each day (Harjanti, 2020). This waste accumulation produces leachate—a thick, dark-colored liquid that carries pollutants and materials from the waste—which has the potential to contaminate the surrounding environment, including the Kreo River. Therefore, phytoremediation using Mendong plants is proposed to reduce the pollutants in the leachate. This research employed an experimental method with a Completely Randomized Design (CRD), using Mendong plants (Fimbristylis globulosa) and three biomass variations: P0 (0 g), P1 (1000 g), and P2 (2000 g). Each treatment involved 10 liters of leachate and was replicated three times. The phytoremediation process proved effective in reducing total ammonia levels in the leachate, with a reduction of up to 63%, and the highest total nitrogen reduction reached 53%. This phytoremediation approach can assist in reducing excess total ammonia in water bodies by absorbing organic pollutants through plant roots, as Mendong exhibits hyperaccumulator and hypertolerant properties. It is concluded that Mendong plants are effective in lowering total ammonia and total nitrogen levels in landfill leachate.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-10454878/v1.abstract: Abstract The transition of the lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) toward industrial application remains a formidable challenge. Achieving stable operation under ampere-level current density is particularly pivotal in this regard. An ideal solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) plays a decisive role in determining the overall efficiency and feasibility. Current research predominantly focuses on bulk electrolyte optimization for SEI control, leaving the direct tailoring of electrode interphase underexplored. This lack of fundamental understanding hinders the achievement of highly efficient and stable Li-NRR toward practical application. Here, we report a strategy to atomic-scale restructure the interfacial microenvironment by engineering Cu substrates with a predominant (220) facet, leveraging the crystallographic orientation to present a definitive pathway for stable interphase. The Cu (220) facet selectively promotes the specific adsorption of anions within the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP), establishing a locally concentrated anion microenvironment even within dilute electrolytes. This facet induced enrichment overrides conventional reduction pathways dominated by solvents, triggering a kinetically accelerated evolution of a thin, robust SEI rich in inorganic components composed primarily of LiF and Li 2 S. This tailored interphase architecture enhances the interfacial Li + diffusion coefficient by two orders of magnitude and shortens the N 2 transport pathway, effectively balancing the transport of Li + , N 2 and H + , enabling the system to sustain a remarkable 1.1 µmol s − 1 cm − 2 ammonia production rate at a sustained current density of -500 mA cm − 2 . This work demonstrates that atomic scale manipulation of substrate crystallography can dictate macroscopic interphase chemistry, charting a robust and scalable pathway for high flux electrochemical synthesis.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11134508/v1.abstract: Abstract Saudi Arabia plans to export green ammonia to Europe and East Asia, but its 2030 demand, its delivered price and the availability of the Suez route are all uncertain. This paper presents a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear program that selects export sites on the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf coasts, sizes the solar, wind, electrolyzer and ammonia synthesis capacity at each, and decides production and shipping to Rotterdam, Japan and Korea in 50 scenarios of demand, price and route state. Renewable supply uses linear supply blocks checked against the NEOM Green Hydrogen project, and all data sources are public. The risk-neutral solution opens NEOM only, with 1.80 Mt/yr of ammonia capacity fed by 4.4 GW of PV, 2.9 GW of wind and 3.6 GW of electrolysis, and an expected annual profit of 160 million USD. The design sized on expected demand and price builds 3.17 Mt/yr at NEOM and Yanbu and has an expected loss of 140 million USD per year, so the value of the stochastic solution is 301 million USD per year; the expected value of perfect information is 199 million USD per year. Gulf sites are not selected because their production cost is about 130 USD/t higher than at NEOM. A strongly risk-averse investor does not invest without price support, while a delivered price floor of 750 USD/t keeps the investment at every level of risk aversion. Expected profit is most sensitive to the price level, the cost of capital and the electrolyzer cost.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-11134508/v1.title: Optimal design of a green ammonia export supply chain from Saudi Arabia under demand, price and route uncertainty: a two-stage stochastic programming approach

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11284169/v1.abstract: Abstract Rational catalyst design for ammonia decomposition requires navigating coupled structural and electronic effects that govern reaction energetics across a large configurational space. Here, we integrate density functional theory (DFT), microkinetic modeling (MKM), and interpretable machine learning to establish a physics-guided screening framework. For the most active stepped Ru(10–13) surface, MKM identifies NH* dissociation as the rate-limiting step and defines an NH* binding-energy window of -4.47 to -3.84 eV that sustains near-maximal turnover frequency across 673–750 K and applied fields of 0 and − 0.4 V/Å. A DFT database comprising 1,132 Ru and 270 Co configurations spanning surface structure, adatom coverage, and electronic state was used to train a gradient-boosted model, achieving a Ru test mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.082 eV. Although direct Ru-to-Co transfer yields a 0.397 eV error, incorporating only 45 Co configurations reduces the Co test MAE to 0.120 eV. SHAP analysis identifies charge, local site coordination, and surface energy as the dominant factors governing NH* binding. Guided by these relationships, screening ~ 33,000 physically constructed candidates enriches the population within the kinetic target, while constrained-DFT validation supports the model’s ability to identify promising configurations.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-11507422/v1.abstract: Abstract Solvent selection can exert a substantial influence on the microstructural development and functional response of oxide thin films prepared by aerosol-based deposition. In this study, nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄) thin films were deposited on glass substrates by nebulizer-assisted spray pyrolysis using water, methanol, ethanol and isopropanol-containing precursor solutions. The resulting films were examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), UV–visible spectroscopy and ammonia (NH₃) sensing measurements. XRD analysis was reported to be consistent with a cubic spinel structure, while the ethanol-containing formulation produced the sharpest diffraction peaks and the largest estimated crystallite size (approximately 24.5 nm). SEM observations indicated a comparatively uniform, porous and less agglomerated surface for the ethanol-derived film. Optical analysis yielded an estimated band gap of approximately 1.86 eV for this sample, lower than the values reported for the water-, methanol- and isopropanol-derived films. The ethanol-derived film also exhibited a concentration-dependent current response to NH₃, with a reported response of approximately 500% at 250 ppm. These findings suggest that solvent composition is a potentially useful processing variable for tailoring the structural, optical and gas-sensing behaviour of spray-pyrolysed NiFe₂O₄ films. Further quantitative validation—including replicate measurements, response and recovery times, selectivity, baseline stability and uncertainty analysis—is required before practical sensor performance can be established.

10.2139/ssrn.7552551.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia proceeds through sequential NO3-→NO2- and NO2-→NH3 transformations, which consume two and six electrons, respectively. Under galvanostatic operation, the fixed total electron flux constrains these coupled steps; however, how their relative kinetics regulate intermediate accumulation and ammonia production remains insufficiently understood. Here, a series of CuxMoy bimetallic electrodes was prepared by electrochemical co-deposition to investigate this relationship. Time-dependent concentration profiles of NO3-, NO2-, and NH3 were fitted using a sequential two-step kinetic model to quantify the apparent kinetics of nitrite formation and consumption. The analysis shows that k1 governs the supply of nitrite, whereas k2 determines its consumption and thereby regulates product distribution. Efficient ammonia production requires matching these two processes: rapid nitrate reduction alone leads to nitrite accumulation when subsequent conversion is insufficient, whereas inadequate nitrate activation limits the intermediate supply for ammonia formation. The optimized Cu0.05Mo0.10 electrode achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 96.9% and an ammonia production rate of 0.33 mmol cm-2 h-1 at 80 mA·cm-2 in 1 M KOH containing 0.05 M NO3-. Material characterization and density functional theory calculations indicate that Cu facilitates nitrate adsorption, while Mo modulates the adsorption of key hydrogenation intermediates. This work establishes a galvanostatic kinetic framework that connects catalyst composition, two-step reaction kinetics, and the use of a finite electron supply in nitrate-to-ammonia conversion.

10.2139/ssrn.7566340.abstract: Although catalytic wet peroxide oxidation (CWPO) effectively remediates organic wastewater, high reagent requirements and slow reaction kinetics limit its practical application. Here, a core-shell Fe3O4@ZIF‒67 catalyst (FOZIF) was synthesized and used in an induction heating-assisted CWPO (IH‒CWPO) system for the rapid and efficient generation of reactive radicals. In this system, induction heating synergistically accelerates H2O2 activation over the FOZIF catalyst to generate abundant hydroxyl radicals. Mechanistically, the electron-donating Fe2+ species in the Fe3O4 core accelerate the Co3+/Co2+ redox cycle within the ZIF-67 shell, establishing a dual Fe/Co active site network. Consequently, the optimized FOZIF‒2 catalyst achieved 98.2% degradation of tetracycline (TC) within 30 min in the IH‒CWPO system, yielding a remarkable rate constant of 1.46 × 10−1 min−1, significantly outperforming conventional CWPO. After four cycles of operation, the TC removal efficiency dropped by only ~16%, confirming the good magnetic recyclability and operational stability of FOZIF‒2 in the IH‒CWPO system. This research highlights the promise of combining electromagnetic heating with MOF-based magnetic catalysts for highly efficient wastewater treatment.

10.2139/ssrn.7571359.abstract: The low electronic conductivity of TiO2 limits its rate capability as a lithium-ion battery anode. Conductive TiO2 was prepared from commercial anatase powder by carbon-cloth-assisted flash Joule heating (FJH). Conductivity increased with treatment temperature and pulse number, reaching 24.32 S cm−1 after 100 pulses at 1500 °C. The resulting material was predominantly rutile. X-ray photoelectron and electron paramagnetic resonance spectra supported oxygen vacancy formation and partial Ti reduction, which may contribute to the increased conductivity. The apparent optical bandgap decreased from 3.30 to 2.02 eV. In lithium half-cells, the treated material delivered approximately 62 mAh g−1 at 20 C and maintained approximately 80 mAh g−1 after 400 cycles at 10 C.

10.2139/ssrn.7576410.abstract: Carbon-based materials attenuate strongly yet suffer from impedance mismatch due to an excessive dielectric response, limiting the lightweight, thin, and broadband absorbers required for electromagnetic protection. Here, graphene sheets were assembled into a nitrogen-doped three-dimensional graphene framework (N-3DG), and the in situ confined growth of high-entropy alloy (FeCoNiCrMn) nanoparticles was achieved via flash Joule heating. The alloy components moderate the excessive dielectric response of the N-3DG framework, allowing incident electromagnetic waves to enter the absorber effectively. Meanwhile, alloy compositional evolution enhances polarization loss and synergistically improves impedance matching and attenuation. The optimized N-3DG/FeCoNiCrMn composite achieves a minimum reflection loss of -62.49 dB at 11.92 GHz with a thickness of 2.06 mm at a filler loading of only 15 wt%, together with an effective absorption bandwidth of at least 5.36 GHz (12.64-18 GHz) at 1.69 mm, whereas pristine N-3DG shows no effective absorption band (RL ≤ -10 dB) over 2-18 GHz. This work clarifies the composition-electromagnetic-response relationship within the investigated alloy series and provides a feasible route to lightweight, low-filler-loading carbon-based absorbers.

10.2139/ssrn.7601276.abstract: Copper-based oxide is a cost-competitive and high-performance catalyst for the photoelectrocatalytic reduction of nitrate to ammonia, but their insufficient stability under negative potentials limits practical applications. A PdO/CuOx@NF photoelectrocathode with synergistic components was fabricated. The CuOx semiconductor enables photocurrent generation and nitrate photoelectrochemical reduction, while Pd species suppress photogenerated charge recombination and modulate interfacial hydrogen adsorption. Electrochemical reconstruction combined with pulsed-potential electrolysis activates and stabilizes Cu and Pd active sites of the PdO/CuOx@NF, enabling efficient photoelectrochemical nitrate reduction to ammonia. The optimized PdO/CuOx@NF catalyst delivers a stable NH3 yield of approximately 110 μg·h-1·cm-2 during 20-hour continuous electrolysis at -0.2 V vs. RHE. Operando XAFS was used to track the evolution of copper phases and unveil the real active sites under different photoelectrolysis modes. The results reveal that electrochemical reconstruction induces the formation of mixed-valence Cu0/Cu+ species, which enables effective synergy between photocatalysis and electrocatalysis. The applied periodic positive bias further stabilizes the catalytic interface and sustains the favorable valence states of Cu oxides and metallic Pd. This work presents a reliable strategy to improve the stability of conventional oxide semiconductors for photoelectrochemical reduction reactions, while retaining their high catalytic activity.

10.2139/ssrn.7629221.abstract: Ammonia co-firing reduces direct CO₂ emissions from coal-fired plants but changes furnace heat transfer, flue-gas losses, and steam-temperature control. This study evaluates a 1,000 MW-class ultra-supercritical once-through coal-fired plant at ammonia energy fractions of 0–100%, with fuel allocation and efficiency calculated using lower heating values (LHVs) at 25°C. Degradation is decomposed into composition and temperature contributions, and ammonia preheating and tuning are assessed within a common plant boundary. At 100% ammonia, net efficiency decreases by 1.22 percentage points (pp) on an LHV basis and 6.24 pp on a higher heating value (HHV) basis relative to coal. First-stage preheating (PH1), controlled to recover the additional sensible exhaust heat caused by the higher flue-gas temperature, restores 59–98% of the temperature-related net-efficiency loss at 20%, 50%, and 100% ammonia under rated-load conditions. Recovery reaches 0.78 pp at 100% ammonia. Second-stage preheating with extraction steam adds 0.23 pp because the boiler gain exceeds the cycle penalty. Combining preheating and tuning restores 1.33 pp and reduces fuel consumption per unit net electricity by 3.02%, while maintaining a spray ratio near 7% at rated load. Preheating and air adjustment improve efficiency, whereas separator outlet enthalpy adjustment restores spray control margin. At subcritical part load, the outlet-superheat requirement restricts this adjustment; at 75% load and 100% ammonia, combined-case spray stays within capacity but reaches about 21% of main-steam flow, above the 14% design ratio. The results link loss decomposition to heat-recovery design; combustion, emission, and equipment constraints require further validation.
10.2139/ssrn.7629221.title: Thermal performance degradation of an ultra-supercritical coal-fired power plant under ammonia co-firing and its recovery through ammonia preheating and operational tuning

10.2139/ssrn.7642974.abstract: In-situ repair of tungsten is hindered by thermal-stress cracking, low forming efficiency, and high cost. This study employed powder extrusion printing (PEP) for in-situ repair and developed a rapid induction heating debinding (RIHD) process integrated with laser cladding to fabricate tungsten thin layers. The effects of feedstock rheology, printing parameters, debinding, and cladding on the forming behavior and microstructural evolution were systematically investigated. The feedstock exhibited typical shear-thinning behavior, with a viscous-flow activation energy of 388.19 J mol⁻¹, indicating low temperature sensitivity and stable processing. An L16(45) orthogonal design clarified the effects of printing parameters on green-body surface roughness and interlayer adhesion. A layer thickness of 0.1 mm effectively suppressed warping and delamination induced by residual thermal stress. Under optimized conditions, the green body achieved a minimum surface roughness of 1.305 μm and an interfacial adhesion strength of 0.251 MPa. RIHD at 950 °C for 20 min yielded a debinding rate of 99.5%, comparable to the 99.7% obtained by conventional thermal debinding. Laser cladding at 400 W produced a dense tungsten layer, demonstrating the potential of the integrated PEP-RIHD-cladding route for efficient in-situ tungsten repair.

10.2139/ssrn.7674319.abstract: ABSTRACT: Electrochemical nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3-RR) enables nitrate removal from contaminated water together with decentralized ammonia production. However, in the near-neutral media commonly encountered in nitrate-containing wastewater, sluggish water dissociation and limited interfacial proton availability severely constrain the reaction kinetics and ammonia production efficiency. To address this challenge, we constructed a Pd-Cu2O metal-metal oxide catalyst featuring synergistic dual active sites (Pd3Cu1/NF). Experimental results demonstrate that the synergistic coupling between Pd and Cu sites regulates interfacial water adsorption and hydrogen-bonding configurations, promotes water activation and the generation and transfer of reactive hydrogen species, and thereby accelerates the consecutive hydrogenation and deoxygenation of nitrate to ammonia. Benefiting from these synergistic effects, Pd3Cu1/NF delivers excellent NO3-RR performance in a near-neutral electrolyte, achieving a Faradaic efficiency of 92% and an ammonia yield rate of 1.36 mmol cm-2 h-1 at -1.2 V versus RHE, which is 2.72 times that of Cu/NF. The catalyst also maintains stable performance over 40 consecutive cycles. This work establishes a broadly applicable metal-metal oxide catalyst design strategy for efficient electrochemical nitrate-to-ammonia conversion under mild conditions through the regulation and effective utilization of interfacial proton supply.

10.2139/ssrn.7674320.abstract: Photocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) offers a sustainable route for ambient ammonia synthesis, but bismuth vanadate (BiVO4) exhibits intrinsically low activity due to rapid charge recombination and poor N2 activation. Herein, a 0D/2D CdS/BiVO4 heterojunction is fabricated via in-situ assembly to boost BiVO4 NRR performance through interfacial engineering. The optimized catalyst achieves an ammonia production rate of 200 μmol g-1 h-1, approximately 16 times higher than that of pristine BiVO4. Quasi in-situ Raman and photoelectrochemical characterizations verify that the intimate heterointerface promotes charge separation and modulates the light-induced evolution of the surface structure. Density functional theory calculations, N2 temperature-programmed desorption, and in-situ Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy reveal that the heterointerface, along with vanadate tetrahedral distortion, modulates the interfacial electronic structure, strengthens N2 adsorption and activation, and thereby lowers the first protonation energy barrier. This work offers insights into the regulation of interfacial activity in bismuth-based NRR photocatalysts.
10.2139/ssrn.7674320.title: Activating Inert BiVO4 Surfaces toward Efficient Photocatalytic Nitrogen Reduction via Interfacial Engineering

10.2139/ssrn.7675398.abstract: Core–shell BiFeO3 (BFO) @Fe3O4 integrates the ferroelectric polarization of BFO with the ferrimagnetic response of Fe3O4, creating an exchange-coupled piezo-magnetoelectric catalyst that converts mechanical stimulation into interfacial redox driving forces. Magnetic-field priming reorients and stabilizes the BFO dipoles through interfacial coupling, with dye oxidation serving as a direct probe of the resulting piezo-magnetoelectric effect. The magnetic squareness (Mr/Ms) of ~0.15 indicates that the Fe3O4 shell retains a remanent magnetic state capable of sustaining interfacial coupling after removal of the external magnetic field. The pronounced dependence of the probe reaction on magnetic-field priming (0–500 Oe) and electrical pre-polarization (0–2.5 V μm-1), with an optimum at 300 Oe and 2 V μm-1, reveals that the mechanically generated redox driving force is governed by coupled magnetic and ferroelectric domain regulation rather than piezoelectric polarization alone. Remarkably, the same field-optimized catalyst also enables reductive nitrogen conversion, with pre-polarized BFO@Fe3O4 achieving a higher nitrate-to-ammonia reduction (NO3RR) rate (6617 µmol L-1 h-1 g cat. -1) than its non-polarized counterpart (4941 µmol L-1 h-1 g cat. -1) under ultrasonic activation. Density functional theory and finite element calculations further reveal that Fe3O4 incorporation regulates interfacial spin alignment, drives charge redistribution, and amplifies the piezoelectric potential, thereby establishing the mechanistic origin of charge separation across oxidative and reductive pathways. These findings identify piezo-magnetoelectric coupling as a previously underexplored mechanism for directing mechanically generated charges toward distinct redox reactions, extending mechanically driven catalysis from radical oxidation to sustainable nitrate-to-ammonia conversion.

10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-g53rc/v3.abstract: We report the synthesis of Fe foams by dynamic hydrogen bubble template (DHBT)-assisted electrodeposition and their electrocatalytic performance for the selective reduction of nitrate to ammonia, a strategy that mitigates nitrate pollution while providing a decentralized route for ammonia production. Fe-foam_90s@Ti achieves a Faradaic efficiency of up to 97% and a partial current density for ammonia formation approaching -1 A cm -2 without externally imposed convection. Operando Raman spectroscopy tracked the potential-dependent reduction of surface Fe oxides and, together with identical-location scanning electron microscopy (IL-SEM), supported the assignment of metallic Fe as the catalytically active state for selective ammonia formation. Potential-dependent ICP-MS and ion chromatography analyses identified an operating window with minimal Fe dissolution, in which the corrosion-prone catalyst can be electrochemically stabilized through cathodic protection. The catalyst was further implemented in a laboratory-scale flow-cell electrolyzer under galvanostatic conditions, demonstrating its compatibility with continuous-flow operation. Together, these results establish DHBT-derived Fe foams as promising electrocatalysts for high-rate ammonia electrosynthesis and support their further evaluation in scaled flow-cell systems.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009696/v2.abstract: Selective catalytic conversion of complex hydrocarbons into light olefins remains challenging because of costly catalyst preparation and catalyst deactivation under severe cracking conditions. Here, we report pulsed Joule heating for highly selective light olefin production from complex hydrocarbon mixtures. By precisely regulating reaction severity, this catalyst-free approach achieves light olefin yields comparable to those reported for catalytic cracking. We systematically characterized the feedstock molecular composition and evaluated olefin yields of diverse hydrocarbon mixtures, including polyolefins, crude oils, Fischer-Tropsch wax, and shale oil. To quantify the effects of pulse parameters on olefin production, we developed a spatiotemporal reactor model based on a quasi-molecular reaction network. The model reveals that pulsed Joule heating regulates high-temperature reactions to match product removal, thereby improving olefin yield and selectivity. Guided by the model, catalyst-free pulsed Joule heating crude oil pyrolysis was optimized and achieved a light olefin yield of approximately 38 wt%. These findings establish a quantitative framework for temporal regulation of complex hydrocarbon pyrolysis and provide a basis for industrial electrified olefin production.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009859/v1.abstract: Selective electrochemical conversion of nitrate (NO 3 - ) to dinitrogen (N 2 ) is attractive for nitrate remediation but remains challenging because competing hydrogenation pathways often yield reduced nitrogen products. Here, we develop a self-supported flexible electrified membrane (α-Co/NC@CNTFEM) by integrating phase-defined hexagonal close-packed (HCP) α-Co/nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) into a conductive carbon nanotube (CNT) framework. The resulting membrane combines a uniformly integrated catalytic phase with a thin, interconnected porous architecture suitable for flow-through electrochemical operation. At an initial nitrate concentration of 10 mg L -1 , α-Co/NC@CNT-FEM achieves 96.5% nitrate conversion, 81.5% N 2 Faradaic efficiency, and 97.9% N 2 selectivity, exceeding the corresponding mixed-phase Co NP /NC@CNT-FEM and bare CNT-FEM. The enhanced N 2 selectivity is associated with the coupled effects of the phase-defined α-Co, N-doped carbon matrix, and flow-through CNT microenvironment, which may favor N–N coupling while suppressing excessive hydrogenation. Moreover, our results also reveal that stable nitrate removal on this platform is maintained over 10 consecutive cycles. This work demonstrates crystal-phase engineering coupled with electrified membrane design as a materials strategy for selective nitrate-to-N 2 conversion.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15009889/v1.abstract: The selective electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3−) to ammonia (NH3) represents a promising route for sustainable NH3 production. However, achieving high NH3 selectivity remains challenging due to competing reactions. Additionally, many reported catalysts rely on noble metals and often require relatively elevated catalyst loadings to achieve high apparent activity, while most systems operate only at relatively low current densities. Herein, a fourteen-membered macrocyclic copper complex supported on Ketjenblack (Cu-14MR/KB) is reported as a cathode catalyst for the highly selective electrochemical reduction of NO3− to NH3. With a low Cu loading of 1.34 μmol cm−2, Cu-14MR/KB delivered a high Faraday efficiency for NH3 synthesis of up to 94.8% at a current density of −26.3 mA cm−2 and maintained high NH3 selectivity over a wide current density range from −26.3 to −150 mA cm−2. Notably, at −150 mA cm−2, Cu-14MR/KB achieved an NH3 yield rate of 604 μmol cm−2 h−1 with an NH3 Faraday efficiency of 86.4%. Furthermore, a more contracted Cu–N4 coordination environment was revealed in Cu-14MR than in CuPc, with a shorter Cu–N bond distance, suggesting relatively stronger Cu–N interactions. This work provides an efficient strategy for high-performance NO3− electroreduction using a low-loading and non-noblemetal catalyst.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010116/v1.abstract: The photoelectrochemical (PEC) nitrogen reduction reaction (N 2 RR) offers a potentially sustainable route to ammonia (NH 3 ) synthesis. However, reliable evaluation of PEC N 2 RR activity remains challenging due to contamination-induced false positives and competing reactions. Here, we comparatively investigate p -type CuBi 2 O 4 and the previously reported PEC N 2 RR-active photocathode CuO, using an ultra-clean, contamination-controlled measurement system. Despite favorable band energetics and measurable photocurrents, neither material exhibits statistically significant NH 3 production, suggesting that the previously reported activity of CuO most likely originated from contamination-induced false positives rather than genuine N 2 reduction. Density functional theory further shows that the first proton-coupled electron transfer step toward *NNH formation remains kinetically prohibitive, even on oxygen-deficient surfaces, strongly favoring the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In addition, both photocathodes undergo surface reduction and photocorrosion. Nevertheless, comparative analysis reveals fundamentally different degradation pathways on the two photocathodes. While CuBi 2 O 4 retains its bulk structural integrity under photocathodic conditions, CuO undergoes extensive reduction, restructuring, and dissolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of contamination control in evaluating aqueous PEC N 2 RR, as well as the challenges of overcoming vigorous competition with HER and photocorrosion processes using Cu(II)-based oxides.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010250/v1.abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) and nitrite participate in intertwined signaling chemistry, yet the factors governing product selectivity between nitric oxide (NO) and nitroxyl (HNO) and the underlying reaction pathways remain poorly defined. Here, we establish that reduction of a zinc-nitrite complex by H 2 S follows stoichiometry-dependent product selectivity. With 2 equiv of H 2 S, the reaction generates NO and HNO-derived nitrous oxide (N 2 O) trapped in 46.3% ± 2.1% and 19.7% ± 1.5%, yields, respectively. UV-vis and 15 N NMR spectroscopy along with phosphine-based intermediate trapping and DFT studies support a nucleophilic attack pathway involving zinc-bound thionitrite (SNO − ) and perthionitrite (SSNO − ) intermediates. We independently synthesize and crystallographically characterize the zinc-perthionitrite complex, identifying isomers with cis-ĸ 2 -S,O and unprecedented Y-shaped ĸ 2 -S,S coordination modes in the solid-state. In contrast, 5 equiv of H 2 S favors an acidbase pathway involving spectroscopically intercepted nitrous acid (HONO) intermediate and affords NO in 94.6% ± 1.5% yield, with only trace N 2 O. Reaction with hydrosulfide (HS − ) instead, generate a zinc-hydrosulfide-nitrite adduct without nitrite reduction; subsequent protonation produces NO exclusively. Together, these findings establish H 2 S stoichiometry and proton availability as complementary determinants of competing nitrite reduction pathways that control NO versus N 2 O selectivity at a redox-inactive zinc center.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010290/v1.abstract: Efficient utilisation of solar UV light ( λ > 300 nm) is essential for practical photocatalytic CO 2 conversion. However, in conventional systems using water as an electron donor, slow water oxidation kinetics present a critical bottleneck that severely limits the CO production rate. Here, we demonstrate an efficient CO 2 conversion system that overcomes this kinetic limitation by employing ammonia as an alternative electron donor over Mg-doped SrTiO 3 loaded with Ag and Fe as dualcocatalysts (Ag–Fe/Mg–SrTiO 3 ). Under UV irradiation ( λ > 300 nm), the optimised photocatalyst achieved a remarkable CO produc on rate exceeding 200 μmol h −1 . Mechanistic investigations revealed that the Fe cocatalyst played a crucial role in promoting ammonia oxidation, facilitating the rapid consumption of photogenerated holes, and significantly enhancing CO 2 conversion activity. Furthermore, nitrite (NO 2 − ) was successfully quantified as the primary oxidation product of ammonia, yielding a calculated e − / h + balance of approximately 1.2, validating the stoichiometric relationship of the reaction. This study offers a promising strategy for simultaneously achieving the upcycling of CO 2 and effective utilisation of ammonia as both an energy source and an electron donor.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010321/v1.abstract: Direct utilization of dinitrogen (N2) in organic synthesis remains an unmet challenge in sustainable chemistry, particularly under mild conditions. Conventional transition-metal-mediated N2 functionalization typically requires elaborately designed catalysts under harsh conditions, limiting operational practicality. Here, we report a mechanochemical strategy that achieves rapid, lithium-mediated N2 reduction at ambient pressure and temperature in under two minutes, delivering polymorphic mixtures of α- and β-lithium nitride. The resulting metal nitride serves as a versatile platform for single nitrogen-atom transfer: applied to skeletal conversion reactions, it enables direct O-to-N transmutation of furans and aromatic oxonium salts into the corresponding pyrroles and pyridine derivatives, establishing a formal incorporation of N2 into N-heterocycles. The photophysical consequences of the single-atom edit on excited-state properties of the molecular chromophores were evaluated.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010462/v1.abstract: Ammonia borane (NH3BH3) is a hydrogen rich molecular solid whose structural behaviour is governed by molecular orientation and N–H· · ·H–B dihydrogen interactions. Its temperature-dependent phase transition is conventionally described as an order–disorder transition from a disordered tetragonal phase to a more ordered orthorhombic phase. However, this description does not fully capture the underlying local structure. Single crystal X-ray diffraction, X-ray total scattering, Pair Distribution Function (PDF) analysis and Reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) modelling reveal an unexpected inversion of local structural order across the phase transition. At 300 K, despite pronounced disorder in the average tetragonal structure, the local structure exhibits three preferential NH3 orientations, whereas the BH3 groups remain substantially disordered. In contrast, at 100 K, modelling reveals substantial local disorder of NH3 despite the more ordered average orthorhombic structure. Single crystal diffraction additionally reveals weak satellite reflections, while the 100 K powder diffraction pattern is better reproduced by a trial commensurately modulated model with threefold periodicity than by the conventional average structure. Together, these results indicate that the low temperature phase combines periodic structural modulation with substantial local disorder, demonstrating that average and local structural order do not evolve in parallel with temperature.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15010462/v1.title: Structural Order Reversed: Local and Average Structure Across the Ammonia Borane Phase Transition

10.26434/chemrxiv.15010463/v1.abstract: The decisive challenge in nitrate-to-ammonia electrosynthesis is not simply supplying electrons, but ensuring that successive nitrogen intermediates remain chemically convertible. Here, we establish a molecular strategy that differentiates framework-derived electronic character from metal-directed reaction selectivity through TU-420, a crystalline covalent organic framework integrating electron-donating tetrathiafulvalene and electron-accepting, metal-coordinating bipyridine units. Electronic-structure analysis identifies complementary donor-associated and acceptor-like states, while Xray absorption spectroscopy reveals distinct approximately six-coordinate Fe–O/N and four-coordinate Cu–O/N environments within the conserved architecture. Remarkably, TU-420-Fe achieves 98.1% ammonia Faradaic efficiency at −0.60 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and an ammonia production rate of 4.33 mg h-1 cm-2 at −0.80 V, whereas TU-420-Cu exhibits substantially lower selectivity despite its stronger cathodic response. Isotope-labeling experiments establish nitrate as the nitrogen source, while in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and differential electrochemical mass spectrometry reveal signatures consistent with evolving nitrogen–oxygen and hydrogenated nitrogen species. Density functional theory identifies the mechanistic distinction: Fe supports a favorable *NHO-mediated reduction sequence with a maximum uphill free-energy increment of 0.30 eV, while substantially alleviating the energetic penalty associated with the competing *NOH-mediated route relative to Cu. These findings identify the energetic fate of partially reduced nitrogen, rather than electron consumption alone, as a determinant of ammonia selectivity and establish electronically differentiated covalent architectures as platforms for programming metal-dependent multielectron catalysis.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15011227/v1.abstract: Many scenarios for the energy transition consider green ammonia. The technologically most mature production process combines water electrolysis and Haber-Bosch process (EHB). Its costs are dominated by electrolyzer investment costs and electricity. Emerging pathways researched in academia, start-ups, and industry try to reduce costs by changing sub-processes and chemistry. However, it remains unclear which pathways have the potential to outperform EHB, if any. We assess relevant emerging pathways, compare to EHB in terms of costs and energy demand, and derive performance targets. Many pathways investigated in the literature, such as metalmediated electrolysis, have theoretical minimal energy demands well above the actual energy demand of EHB; consequently, they cannot produce ammonia at competitive costs due to the high influence of electricity costs. Any novel pathway must employ simple and energy-effective chemistry to substantially reduce costs. Identified performance targets are applicable to novel pathways and can guide research, industry, and policy makers.

10.26599/nr.2026.94908876.abstract: Abstract The electrocatalytic reduction of nitric oxide (NO) to ammonia (NH3) (NORR) provides a sustainable solution for pollutant remediation and value-added chemical synthesis. In this study, we introduce porous aromatic frameworks (PAFs) into the NORR system for the first time, exploiting their unique channel structures to enhance gas adsorption and mass transport. By incorporating Co2+ ions into the PAF-TPP material, constructed from tetraphenylporphyrin (TPP), we created the PAF-TPP-Co catalyst, which offers active coordination sites. The PAF structure effectively regulates the interfacial enrichment of NO molecules and promotes mass transport, while the synergistic effect between the Co-N4 active sites and the PAF framework optimizes both electronic structure and material transport. Through the combined action of microporous structure and active sites, PAF-TPP-Co significantly improves NO adsorption and transport efficiency, facilitating the multi-electron conversion of NO to NH3. At a potential of −0.6 V vs. RHE, this catalyst achieves an ammonia production rate of 914.2 μg·h−1·mgcat−1 and a Faradaic efficiency of 71.3%. Moreover, we propose a “adsorption-transport-catalysis” synergistic mechanism that not only enhances NO activation but also suppresses the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction. In situ infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to further elucidate the catalytic mechanism. This study offers a new mechanistic perspective on NO electrocatalytic reduction based on PAF materials and provides an effective solution for the “waste-to-resource” conversion of industrial NO emissions.

10.26599/nr.2026.94909171.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic ammonia oxidation reaction (EAOR) remains hindered by the lack of catalysts that simultaneously achieve high activity and long-term stability. Herein, we report a surface compositional gradient PtFe alloy catalyst (G-PtFe) consisting of a Pt-Fe gradient shell and a PtFe alloy core. The G-PtFe delivers an EAOR current density of 541.7 mA·cm−2, representing an 8.7-fold improvement over pristine Pt, while exhibiting robust poisoning resistance across a wide potential range of 0.5–1.2 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). When employed as anode catalyst in direct ammonia fuel cells, the G-PtFe-based device achieves a peak power density 3.3 times higher than that of commercial Pt/C. Combined experimental analyses and density functional theory simulations reveal that EAOR deactivation on conventional Pt-based catalysts originates from potential-dependent adsorption imbalance: insufficient surface OH adsorption at low potentials promotes the accumulation of N-containing poisoning intermediates, whereas excessive OH binding at high potentials suppresses NH3 adsorption and induces surface passivation. The surface compositional gradient structure enables dynamically balanced OH and NH3 adsorption over a wide potential window, resulting in ultra-stable EAOR performance. This work provides mechanistic insights into potential-dependent catalyst poisoning and establishes a surface gradient alloy strategy for rational design of efficient and durable EAOR catalysts.

10.26599/pom.2026.9140169.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate(NO3-) reduction technology can simultaneously realize the remediation of nitrate pollution in water and distributed ammonia(NH3) synthesis. To meet the demand for efficient nitrate removal and ammonia resource recovery under practical water treatment conditions, it is of great significance to develop high-performance NO3- electroreduction catalysts suitable for near-neutral environments. However, the sluggish kinetics of multi-proton-coupled electron transfer in neutral media typically lead to unsatisfactory ammonia yields. To handle this issue, we design the lacunary polyoxometalate(POM)-modified Ag-Au nanoalloy catalysts supported by activated-carbon (10% AuAg-SiW9/C) to achieve efficient electrocatalytic conversion of NO3--to-NH3 under neutral conditions. The highly negative-charged SiW9 polyoxoanion effectively stabilized and dispersed the ultrafine AgAu alloy nanoparticles (~6 nm) through strong electrostatic repulsion. In 1 M phosphate buffer at pH ~7.4 containing 0.1 M KNO3, 10% AuAg-SiW9/C delivers a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 95% and an NH3 yield rate of 1.3963 mg h-1 cm-2 at −0.6 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The synergistic effect between the SiW9 polyoxoanions and Au alloying modulates the surface electronic structure of the Ag host via interfacial charge transfer. Density functional theory calculations elucidate that Au doping coupled with SiW9 incorporation reduces the energy barrier for the *NO → *NOH step to 0.46 eV, significantly facilitating this rate-determining step during the multistep hydrogenation process. This study confirms an effective electronic modulation strategy by coupling POMs modification and alloying effect for enhancing the NO3RR performance of metal-based electrocatalysts, providing new insights into the high-value conversion of nitrogen pollutants and the design of materials for electrochemical NH3 synthesis.

10.26599/pom.2026.9140170.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (ENRA) offers a sustainable strategy for simultaneously mitigating nitrate pollution and producing green ammonia under ambient conditions. However, its efficiency is severely limited by sluggish multi-electron transfer kinetics and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), particularly due to insufficient regulation of interfacial active hydrogen species (*H). Polyoxometalates (POMs) feature abundant oxygen-rich sites capable of reversible protonation, thereby serving as an effective source of *H. Here, we report a POMs-modulated Cu2O–Cu catalyts that enables synergistic regulation of interfacial electron distribution and *H availability. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms pronounced electron transfer between POMs and Cu2O–Cu, while electrochemical analyses reveal that POMs modification significantly enhances the adsorption and storage capacity of *H, thereby promoting nitrate activation and hydrogenation. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations further reveal that POMs-induced interfacial charge redistribution optimizes nitrate intermediate adsorption and lowers the energy barrier of key proton-coupled electron transfer steps, thereby accelerating the ENRA pathway. As a result, the optimized catalyst delivers a high ammonia yield of 36.5 mg h−1 mgcat.−1 and excellent Faradaic efficiency of 97.4%. This work provides a general strategy for constructing POMs-based electrocatalysts via interfacial electron and hydrogen regulation, offering new insights into the rational design of selective ENRA systems.

10.3390/batteries12100416.abstract: The research demonstrates a national project combining solar photovoltaics with second-life automotive lithium batteries for local-scale agricultural irrigation and greenhouse climate control. The auto-opening greenhouse system can adapt to various climate conditions in resource-limited areas. Applying in-house battery management system (BMS) based on adaptive control algorithm, it allows real-time monitoring and prediction of critical parameters such as effective capacity and safety, ensuring safe operation and longer battery life. Results show that, with optimized management, the lifespan of second-life batteries can be extended by an additional 7.8–9.3 years, achieving a maximum discharge power of 3.3 kW while keeping thermal control deviations within 0.3%. Both grid-connected and stand-alone microgrid setups have been successfully tested in the field, improving local energy independence and reducing reliance on external power sources. In addition, to avoid the harm of chemical fertilizers to the environment, air nitrogen fixation technology is employed to extract nitrogen fertilizer from the air to irrigate crops such as tomatoes and cucumbers. The control system uses solar power to store electricity in batteries daily to provide nitrogen fixation and basic greenhouse needs, and can maintain greenhouse operations without relying on power grid. This work offers a practical, scalable model for low-carbon agricultural energy solutions, reducing carbon emissions by about 1.28 metric tons of CO2 per system each year. It provides a framework to guide policies, promote low-carbon transitions, and support global sustainable development goals in underserved areas.

10.3390/gels12110984.abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction can combine nitrogen removal with ammonia recovery, but the contribution of an aerogel network is difficult to separate from changes in catalyst chemistry and electrode preparation. This review examines when the architecture created by gelation and drying remains relevant after electrode fabrication and during nitrate conversion. Metallic, carbon-based, and hybrid aerogels are compared through their preparation, working-state structure, reaction evidence, and operating conditions. Particular attention is given to nitrate activation, downstream hydrogenation, soluble-intermediate retention, and competition with hydrogen evolution and nitrogen formation. Related non-aerogel studies provide mechanistic and reactor comparisons while retaining their distinct material identities. The analysis separates measured responses from proposed pathways and distinguishes peak Faradaic efficiency from sustained conversion and product recovery. Dry surface area, isolated spectroscopic signals, and performance measured under different conditions do not independently establish an aerogel-specific advantage. Priorities emerging from the literature are comparisons of retained and fragmented networks, coupled measurements of intermediate transport and catalyst reconstruction, and nitrogen balances under defined feed and recovery conditions. These comparisons provide a basis for evaluating which aerogel design features remain useful in a working nitrate-conversion device.

10.3390/hydrogen7040168.abstract: This study investigates the integration of Haber–Bosch waste-heat recovery with solid oxide electrolysis (SOE) and evaluates its techno-economic implications through the comparison of stand-alone SOE, hybrid SOE–AWE, and stand-alone AWE hydrogen production configurations. The HB synthesis loop was first simulated and analyzed to quantify the residual heat available after internal heat recovery and assess its thermal suitability for SOE steam generation. The recoverable HB heat initially covers 55% of the SOE evaporator duty. Further optimization of the SOE-side heat-exchanger network using Aspen Energy Analyzer V14 increases this coverage to 63%, enabling SOE to thermally support up to 63% of the hydrogen demand. Additional heat integration opportunities identified using Aspen Energy Analyzer (AEA) increase this coverage to 63%, enabling the SOE system to supply up to 63% of the hydrogen demand. The remaining hydrogen production requirement is investigated under two distinct configurations: (i) a stand-alone SOE system with an internal steam generation unit and (ii) a hybrid configuration consisting of 63% SOE and 37% AWE. These SOE-based configurations are evaluated and compared with a conventional alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) system. The energy analysis demonstrates that SOE-based systems significantly reduce overall energy consumption due to their higher electrochemical efficiency and effective utilization of industrial waste heat. The economic assessment yields LCOH values of 3.90, 3.44, and 2.79 $/kg H2 for the stand-alone SOE, hybrid SOE–AWE, and stand-alone AWE configurations, respectively. 10.3390/jcs10100537.abstract: Shape memory epoxy composites recover a programmed shape when Joule heating drives the matrix through its glass transition, and a key challenge for these smart materials is predicting the recovery angle at drive currents outside the tested range. In this work, three models were compared for this task: a Kohlrausch–Williams–Watts (KWW) theory based Physics-KWW constitutive model, a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost) using thermomechanical state features, and a support vector regression (SVR) model using raw experimental variables together with thermomechanical features. All models were assessed by a leave-one-current-out cross-validation method over nine current levels from 1.50 to 3.50 A. The physics-informed models generalized well to unseen currents, with the Physics-KWW model and XGBoost achieving R2 values of 0.911 and 0.915, respectively, compared with 0.841 for the SVR model under the same tuning protocol. Shapley analysis of a representative XGBoost fold identifies accumulated activation and estimated temperature as the dominant predictors. The results demonstrate comparable accuracy for the two physics-informed approaches, while their advantages remain conditional on the tested pipelines and calibration assumptions.

10.3390/ma19204402.abstract: Metal nanoparticles supported on carbon nanofibers (CNFs) are promising for catalytic and electrochemical applications, but controlling their size, dispersion, and phase during rapid thermal processing remains challenging. Here, we report a dual-solvent microwave carbothermal shock (CTS) method for producing Cu- and Ni-containing nanostructures on CNFs under ambient-pressure conditions. Ethanolic metal nitrate precursors were deposited on pristine CNFs, and hexane was introduced as an antisolvent before microwave irradiation. At 0.05 M Cu(NO3)2, hexane addition decreased the mean Cu-containing particle diameter from 50 ± 20 nm to 33 ± 12 nm and improved dispersion. Varying precursor concentration further altered particle morphology and aggregation. For Ni, single-solvent processing yielded aggregated nanoparticles averaging 43 ± 16 nm, whereas dual-solvent processing produced a dense carbon nanotube network with an apparent mean filament diameter of 20 ± 7 nm. Microscopy and elemental mapping supported the association of Ni-containing particles with the nanotubes. X-ray diffraction identified crystalline face-centered cubic Cu and Ni, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated oxidized surface species. Hexane may additionally supply carbon during Ni-assisted nanotube growth, although its contribution requires confirmation. This approach provides a rapid, tunable route to supported metal nanoparticles and hierarchical carbon nanostructures without continuous external inert or hydrocarbon gas flow.

10.3390/nitrogen7040115.abstract: Morocco’s semi-arid farms are under growing pressure to lower nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions while maintaining crop yields and soil health. Agriculture is a major anthropogenic source of N2O emissions in Morocco; improved nitrogen management is therefore relevant to the country’s broader climate mitigation efforts. This review examines regulatory, technical, and economic measures that have reduced nitrogen losses or agricultural N2O emissions in other countries and assesses their potential relevance to Morocco’s smallholder-dominated farming systems. In 2018, Moroccan managed soils released 13,108 Gg of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-eq) according to the national inventory, highlighting the importance of improved nitrogen management for agricultural climate mitigation. The study compares peer-reviewed research, policy documents, and regulatory frameworks from four benchmark countries: Denmark, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Brazil. It addresses three questions: which nitrogen management strategies have evidence of reducing agricultural N2O emissions in contexts relevant to Morocco; which institutional, regulatory, and socioeconomic barriers may constrain their adoption; and how these strategies could be incorporated into a phased national framework. For each intervention, the review synthesizes reported outcomes, the agronomic and climatic conditions under which they were obtained, and their potential transferability to Morocco’s semi-arid agricultural systems. Outcomes are differentiated as direct N2O measurements, nitrogen loss or fertilizer use indicators, agronomic feasibility evidence, or policy and enabling evidence. The review also identifies gaps in Morocco’s fertilizer governance under Law No. 53-18 and considers national enabling assets, including soil fertility mapping, emerging organic-fertilizer supply chains, conservation agriculture initiatives, and existing agricultural-support programmes. The review presents an author-proposed Integrated Nitrogen Management Framework (INMF) based on three complementary pillars: regulatory reform, field-level technical measures, and economic instruments. It presents three implementation periods—2027–2029, 2029–2032, and 2032–2035—for testing, validating, and progressively scaling these measures under Moroccan conditions. The INMF is a conceptual, phased implementation framework rather than a quantitative national mitigation model. It does not estimate an aggregate agricultural N2O emission reduction because the reviewed interventions differ in their production context, evidence type, and measured outcome. Morocco’s unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) provides the broader policy context, but its economy-wide target is not interpreted as a sector-specific target for agricultural N2O emissions. The review discusses implementation challenges, including data limitations, institutional capacity constraints, and smallholder adoption barriers. It identifies priorities for Morocco: field measurement of N2O emissions and emission factors, multi-site evaluation of mitigation practices, strengthened monitoring and advisory systems, and socioeconomic assessment of farmer adoption and policy feasibility.

10.3390/nitrogen7040124.abstract: Organic nitrogen sources have been widely adopted for rice–wheat cropping systems (RWCSs) of the Indo-Gangetic Plains, but their combined energy, greenhouse-gas and economic performance is rarely assessed. In a fixed-plot experiment at the ICAR Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi, in which the same treatments have been applied since 2002, we compared six organic nitrogen treatments, from an unfertilized control (T1) to green manure plus farmyard manure (FYM) plus biofertilizer (T6). Yield, energy, greenhouse-gas and economic data came from the two most recent rice–wheat cycles; soil organic carbon was measured after the final wheat harvest. Organic inputs raised rice-equivalent yield by 20–50% and total organic carbon by 53–77% relative to the control but increased energy input up to 4.3-fold, so energy-use efficiency fell from 16.4 to 5.3–9.0. The field-scale, gate-to-gate carbon footprint (yield-scaled N2O, CH4, and CO2 emissions) was the lowest in the control (0.27 kg CO2-eq kg−1 grain), the lowest among the amended treatments in green manure plus biofertilizer without FYM (T4; 0.31), and the highest with FYM (0.43–0.48). T4 also had the highest benefit–cost ratio (10.6), and the FYM treatments had ratios of 1.2–1.7 at the recorded FYM price, but this disadvantage depended strongly on the FYM price. A TOPSIS ranking based on five non-redundant criteria placed T4 first; T4 ranked first in 59% of random weight sets and in 89% of uncertainty simulations, with the control being its main competitor. An exploratory data envelopment analysis found no FYM-based treatment to be efficient. Nutritional output increased steadily with organic input and was the highest in T6. Under the conditions of this experiment and the criteria selected, green manure plus biofertilizer offered the most favourable compromise among productivity, efficiency, greenhouse-gas intensity and profitability, whereas FYM-based systems maximized yield and soil carbon at higher calculated energy input and cash cost.

10.3390/nitrogen7040127.abstract: Rice is one of the most nitrogen-demanding staple crops, yet a large proportion of applied nitrogen fertilizer is lost via leaching, volatilization, and denitrification, resulting in low nitrogen use efficiency, increased production costs, and environmental pollution. This situation highlights the urgent need for sustainable strategies that improve nitrogen management and enhance stress resilience in rice systems. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge on the role of plant biostimulants in advancing nitrogen management and sustainability in rice cultivation. We first clarify the definition of plant biostimulants in light of recent international regulations and scientific consensus, emphasizing that they are not direct nutrient sources but substances and microorganisms that stimulate natural plant processes to improve nutrient uptake and stress tolerance. Their agronomic and environmental benefits are discussed, with emphasis on improved root system architecture, enhanced nitrogen uptake, assimilation and remobilization, increased photosynthetic efficiency, and the mitigation of nitrogen losses, which collectively contribute to a reduced environmental footprint. A central part of this review summarizes recent evidence on the application of non-microbial biostimulants for improving nitrogen metabolism and abiotic stress tolerance, microbial biostimulants for biological nitrogen fixation and nutrient solubilization, synergistic effects of combined microbial inoculants, and promising alternative and emerging biostimulant materials in rice. Safety considerations and regulatory frameworks governing the use of these products are also addressed. Overall, the literature indicates that biostimulants represent a practical and environmentally sound approach to support nitrogen management, improve stress resilience, and promote sustainability in rice production. Future research should focus on optimizing formulation, dose, and application timing, and on integrating biostimulants with precision nitrogen fertilization under diverse field conditions.

10.3390/sci8100295.abstract: Nitrate contamination of aquatic environments and the high energy and carbon intensity of conventional ammonia production represent two major and increasingly interconnected sustainability challenges. Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3RR) provides a compelling opportunity to address both by converting a widespread nitrogen pollutant into a value-added chemical and potential energy carrier under comparatively mild conditions. However, practical NO3RR remains constrained by sluggish multistep proton–electron transfer, competing hydrogen evolution, complex nitrogen-containing intermediates, and insufficient control over ammonia selectivity. High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles have recently emerged as a promising catalyst platform for overcoming these limitations because their multielement compositions generate diverse adsorption sites, lattice strain, and tunable electronic interactions that can regulate the binding and transformation of key NO3RR intermediates. This review critically examines the emerging role of HEA nanoparticles in electrocatalytic nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, with emphasis on the relationships among composition, local atomic structure, intermediate adsorption, and catalytic selectivity. Major synthetic strategies, including carbothermal shock, sputtering-based deposition, and wet-chemical co-reduction, are evaluated in terms of their ability to control elemental distribution, particle size, phase stability, and accessible active sites. Particular attention is devoted to mechanistic pathways involving *NO2, *NO, *NHx, and *NH2OH species and to how multimetallic surface environments redirect reaction pathways toward NH3 while suppressing N2, N2O, and H2 formation. Reported Faradaic efficiencies, ammonia production rates, stability, and nitrate-conversion metrics are further benchmarked against conventional monometallic and bimetallic catalysts. Beyond activity under model electrolyte conditions, this review highlights critical knowledge gaps associated with realistic nitrate-contaminated waters, coexisting ions, catalyst reconstruction and metal leaching, long-term stability, energy efficiency, ammonia recovery, and techno-economic scalability. By integrating environmental remediation with decentralized ammonia synthesis, HEA nanoparticles offer a versatile materials framework for advancing nitrate electroreduction toward practically relevant and circular nitrogen-management technologies.

10.5070/rj5.64252.abstract: In order to enhance biochar’s adsorption efficiency for ammonia removal, it must first undergo acid activation, a process in which the surface chemistry of the biochar is altered. Although acid activation is known to increase ammonia adsorption capacity, the effects of specific preparation parameters are not well understood. During activation, biochar is soaked in phosphoric acid and then rinsed to remove residual unbound acid, which could otherwise react with ammonia and interfere with future adsorption measurements. This study focuses on the acid activation step for woodchip biochar pyrolyzed at 500 °C for 15 minutes. Three parameters were investigated: particle size (ground vs. unground), phosphoric acid concentration (15%, 30%, and 45%), and rinsing method (two rinses, five rinses, or a one-hour soak using 20 mL of DI water). pH was measured before and after treatment and used as an indicator of potential ammonia adsorption. To increase readability, the experiment was repeated twice, and samples were prepared at 1 g per condition, resulting in 18 combinations. According to preliminary results, post-activation pH values ranged from 2.2–3.3, whereas initial values ranged from 7.87–9.78. Unground biochar strains consistently showed lower pH values than their ground counterparts, likely due to the difference in particle size. Samples treated with higher acid concentrations (45%) produced lower pH values than those treated with 15% acid, which is consistent with expected trends.

10.55544/sjmars.5.5.5.abstract: Ammoniacal nitrogen is a pervasive aquatic contaminant that threatens aquatic life, compromises disinfection, and drives eutrophication, yet most adsorption studies address concentrations far above those found in natural waters and polished effluents. This study evaluates sugarcane bagasse-derived biochar (SCBC), pyrolysed at [500] °C, as a low-cost adsorbent for ammonia removal at low initial concentrations ([2–30] mg L-1). The biochar was characterised by proximate analysis, pHpzc, BET, FTIR, and XRD, and batch experiments examined the effects of pH, dose, contact time, initial concentration, and temperature. Kinetic data were interpreted using pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, Elovich, and intraparticle diffusion models, and equilibrium data using the Langmuir, Freundlich, Temkin, and Dubinin–Radushkevich isotherms, with model suitability judged by R2, chi-square, and RMSE. Optimum removal of [82]% occurred at pH [7] with a dose of [2] g L-1, and equilibrium was reached within approximately [120] min. The pseudo-second-order model (R2 = [0.998]) and the Langmuir isotherm (R2 = [0.999]) provided the best fits, yielding a maximum monolayer capacity of [12.7] mg g-1. Thermodynamic analysis indicated a spontaneous and endothermic process, and the mean free energy of [10.2] kJ mol-1 pointed to ion exchange, complemented by electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and pore filling. The biochar retained [about 77]% of its efficiency after [five] regeneration cycles. These findings demonstrate that sugarcane biochar is a sustainable, economical option for polishing ammonia-contaminated water at low concentration, while valorising agricultural residue.

10.55763/ippr.2026.07.04.003.abstract: Three developments in 2026 frame the argument of this paper. On April 6, the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam achieved first criticality. Three weeks earlier, missiles struck the Ras Laffan industrial complex in Qatar, and by late April India was contracting urea imports at close to twice the price prevailing in February. On June 26, the Department of Atomic Energy inaugurated a facility producing hydrogen from the copper-chlorine thermochemical cycle using process heat drawn from the Fast Breeder Test Reactor, the first such installation anywhere in the world. India’s urea import dependence rests on the Haber-Bosch process, which requires a large and continuous supply of hydrogen, and that hydrogen is at present made from natural gas. Nuclear process heat offers a different route to that hydrogen, and India has now demonstrated the core of it at bench and pilot scale. This paper does not argue that India should build integrated nuclear-fertiliser complexes now. It argues something narrower. The greater part of India’s planned nuclear capacity is still in the designing stage, and decisions being taken today about reactor design, site allocation, environmental clearance and the rules under the SHANTI Act, 2025 will determine whether integration remains available as a future choice or becomes practically foreclosed. This paper tries establishing six provisions that would keep the option open. Each is inexpensive to adopt now, and difficult or impossible to add once a reactor has been built and licensed.

10.64898/2026.10.12.758474.abstract: Abstract A novel bacterial strain (KR4-4ᵀ), was isolated from soil in the Republic of Korea and subjected to polyphasic taxonomic and functional characterization. Phylogenetic analysis based on the 16S rRNA gene sequence placed strain KR4-4ᵀ within the genus Neobacillus . Phylogenomic analysis based on 92 bacterial core genes further supported its distinct taxonomic position. Average nucleotide identity and digital DNA–DNA hybridization values between KR4-4ᵀ and related Neobacillus type strains were 69.76–82.31% and 18.3–25.9%, respectively, supporting its recognition as a distinct species. Cells were Gram-stain-positive, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic rods, with growth occurring at 15–45 °C, pH 6.0–8.0, and 0–2.0% (w/v) NaCl. The major cellular fatty acids were iso-C 15:0 and anteiso-C 15:0 , while the major polar lipids included diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, and phosphatidylethanolamine. Genome analysis revealed genes associated with inorganic nitrogen transport, nitrate and nitrite reduction, and ammonium assimilation. In liquid culture, KR4-4ᵀ removed NH₄⁺-N under aerobic conditions and was able to utilize ammonium, nitrate, and nitrite as individual nitrogen sources, with removal efficiencies of 86.5%, 69.35%, and 62.9%, respectively. The strain also contributed to the reduction of gaseous NH₃ in a closed-flask assay. Together, these physiological and genomic characteristics indicate a versatile capacity for inorganic nitrogen utilization and transformation and suggest potential for further evaluation in biological ammonia-mitigation applications. Based on phylogenetic, genomic, phenotypic, and chemotaxonomic evidence, strain KR4-4ᵀ represents a novel species of the genus Neobacillus , for which the name Neobacillus ammoniiphilus sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is KR4-4ᵀ (= KACC 24003ᵀ = CCTCC AB 2025077ᵀ). Importance Neobacillus species occur in diverse environments, but their capacity to use and transform multiple inorganic nitrogen forms remains poorly characterized. This study describes Neobacillus ammoniiphilus sp. nov. strain KR4-4ᵀ and links its taxonomic and genomic features with physiological nitrogen-utilization phenotypes. The strain used ammonium, nitrate, and nitrite as individual nitrogen sources, showed substantial ammonium removal under aerobic conditions, and enhanced the reduction of gas-phase ammonia in a sealed-flask assay. Genome analysis identified systems associated with inorganic nitrogen transport, nitrate and nitrite reduction, ammonium assimilation, and nitrogen regulation. These findings expand knowledge of nitrogen metabolism within Neobacillus and identify KR4-4ᵀ as a candidate for further evaluation in biological ammonia-mitigation applications.

arxiv:2610.15798.abstract: Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is among the most promising techniques to provide hydrogen as both energy carrier and feedstock for the chemical industry, due to its compatibility with intermittent renewable electricity sources. However, a major bottleneck in scaling up PEMWE is the limited supply of the anode catalyst Ir. This work shows a novel approach to tailoring ionomer-free catalyst layers based on custom-made microporous substrates and two different atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes, both using Ir(EtCp)(CHD) precursor. Thermal ALD using O3 as counter-reactant yields mostly metallic Ir/IrOx and an electrode Ir loading of 0.21 mg/cm2. The PEMWE cell-level performance is comparable to a commercial catalyst-coated membrane anode despite 7x lower loading, and is maintained over an accelerated durability test equivalent to 600 h of intermittent operation. Moreover, using a low-loading ALD-made cathode, the total platinum group metal loading is only 0.24 mg/cm2. Plasma-enhanced ALD reduces the Ir loading to 0.04 mg/cm2 by tailoring the catalyst distribution, however, yields lower-activity IrO2. Finally, direct ALD catalyst deposition needs no ionomer-bearing ink. The anodes are therefore compatible with various membrane materials, as demonstrated in a CO2 electrolysis experiment with an anion exchange membrane.
